=== PROMPT.md ===
# Editorial playbook — AI Edge Briefing

You are producing today's edition of a daily briefing on frontier AI. The reader uses this as their single place to stay at the edge: the advances, the research, and how AI is being used for good and for harm — cyber, influence ops, military, health, science, policy. It is not a "fun uses of AI" newsletter. It is raw, factual, sourced.

The reader's standard: **every claim links to where it came from, every number is the number in the source, and nothing is written that the sources do not say.** If you cannot source it, it does not go in.

## 0. Setup

1. Work in the repo root. Determine today's date in **America/Toronto**: `TZ=America/Toronto date +%F`. That is the edition date, `DATE`.
2. `ls data/` — the previous edition tells you the cutoff. The coverage window (`WINDOW`) is from the previous edition's `generated_at` to now (if there is no previous edition, the 24 hours before now). Write it down as absolute timestamps in both UTC and ET; you will hand it to the subagents. Read the previous edition so you do not repeat it; a story already covered goes in again **only if there is a new development**, flagged `update`, and the bullets report only the new facts.
3. `node scripts/build.js --topics` — the existing topic slugs. Reuse them; only coin a new slug when nothing fits.
   `node scripts/build.js --storylines` — the open storylines (id, status, name, frame). An item that is a development in one of those arcs is **filed under it** (see §3, `storylines`). The daily never creates a storyline; the Monday Week in Review does.
4. Every day is a daily edition, Mondays included. The week in review is a separate weekly edition with its own playbook (`PROMPT-WEEK.md`) and its own routine — never part of the daily file.

## 0b. Keep your own context small — it is most of what this edition costs

Every turn you take re-sends this whole conversation. So the price of anything you pull into your context
is its size **times the number of turns that come after it** — a page you open early is paid for a hundred
times over. Measured: writing the edition costs about $3; re-reading the conversation while writing it costs
about $20. None of the rules below cost you a source, a check or an item. They stop you paying rent on text
you have already used.

1. **Write files with `Write`, and change them with `Edit`.** Never `cat > file <<'EOF'`, and never a
   `python3 -`/`node -e` script that does find-and-replace on a data file — those put the whole file, or
   whole paragraphs twice over, into the conversation as a command argument. `Edit` sends only the line that
   changes.
2. **Never print a file back out after writing it.** You know what you wrote. To check it, run the
   validator — it prints errors, not contents.
3. **Read the part you need.** `sed -n '40,80p'` over `cat` for anything long, and don't re-read a file
   that has not changed since you read it.
4. **`node scripts/fetch.js` caps its output at 12,000 characters** — the claim, the date and the figures
   are at the top of a page. Add `--full` only when you have looked and what you need is genuinely further
   down. Don't pipe it through `head` as well; the cap is already there.
5. **Let the subagents hold the raw material.** A beat opens fifty pages and hands you back a page of facts;
   that is the whole point of them. When you need a page opened and checked, and a subagent can do it,
   prefer that to opening it yourself.
6. Same rules for the subagents you launch — put a short version of this in every prompt you give them.

None of this licenses checking less. If a fact needs a source opened, open it. Verify everything §2 says to
verify. This is about what you keep afterwards, not what you look at.

## 1. Sweep the sources — four beats in parallel

Read `SOURCES.md`. Then launch **four general-purpose subagents in one message** with the Agent tool, one per beat. Give each: the `WINDOW` as absolute timestamps, its beat's source list from `SOURCES.md`, the **Sourcing rules** below verbatim, and the return format. Tell each to run many searches (15–30) and to open the listed primary sources directly. If the Agent tool is unavailable, work the four beats yourself in turn — do not skip any.

- **Beat A — Frontier models & labs · Compute, chips & infrastructure · Deployment & impact (industry, funding, labor).** SOURCES.md §1, §7, §8.
- **Beat B — Research & papers (incl. safety, alignment, evals).** SOURCES.md §2. arXiv new listings (cs.AI, cs.LG, cs.CL, cs.CR, cs.CV, cs.RO), Hugging Face papers, alphaXiv, Nature/Science, lab research blogs, Epoch, METR, AISI, CAISI, Apollo, Redwood, Alignment Forum. Prefer papers with a notable quantitative result, from major labs/universities, or drawing significant attention. Return arXiv IDs and author institutions.
- **Beat C — Security, misuse & threat intelligence · Military, defense & geopolitics.** SOURCES.md §3, §4. AI-enabled intrusions and malware, fraud and scams, deepfakes, influence operations, surveillance, prompt injection and agent exploits, model theft / illicit distillation, bio/chem misuse reports; procurement, deployment, autonomous weapons, export controls, national strategies.
- **Beat D — Health, science & medicine · Policy, regulation & law.** SOURCES.md §5, §6. Clinical results, FDA/Health Canada/WHO actions, drug discovery, AI for science, biosecurity; legislation, regulation, enforcement, court rulings and filings, government reports, standards — US federal and state, EU, UK, Canada, China, international bodies.

**Subagent return format** — one block per item, then a short list of rejected candidates and why:

```
SECTION: <one of the eight section names>
HEADLINE: <factual, specific, max 18 words, no hype>
PUBLISHED: <date/time and timezone exactly as the source shows it>
SOURCES: one per line — <publisher> | <exact URL> | primary or report   (only URLs actually opened or seen in search results; never constructed)
FACTS: 2–5 bullets, each a verifiable fact from a linked source, numbers/units/baselines exactly as written, naming which source
FLAGS: company-claim | single-source | preprint | update  (any that apply)
```

**Sourcing rules (give to subagents verbatim):**
1. Only include facts that appear in a source you opened (WebFetch) or in the text of a search result. No inference, speculation, predictions or "this could mean". No hype adjectives.
2. Every item links to the specific article, paper or document — never a homepage or index page. Link the primary source whenever one exists (paper, company post, government document, filing, court record) plus independent reporting. Aim for 2+ sources on significant items; if only one outlet has it, flag `single-source`.
3. Confirm the publication date is inside the window. If the date cannot be determined, drop the item. Older stories qualify only if something new happened inside the window, and only the new facts are reported (flag `update`).
4. Attribute claims: "OpenAI says…", "according to The Record…". Company-reported benchmarks, user counts, revenue and capability claims get `company-claim` unless independently verified. Research that is not peer reviewed gets `preprint`.
5. Quote numbers exactly as the source writes them, with units and the comparison baseline. Do not round, convert or compute new figures.
6. If `WebFetch` refuses a page, fetch it directly with `node scripts/fetch.js <url>` — the sites we read have given permission for direct reads, and the fetcher identifies itself. Use only what the returned text actually says; if it comes back as a paywall stub, a login page or nothing usable, fall back to search-result text or another source and say in the bullet where the figures came from. Never use archive or cache sites, and never cite a URL whose content you did not see. Sites that refuse `WebFetch` are listed in SOURCES.md.
7. Skip consumer tips, "fun uses", prompt guides, listicles, opinion pieces without new facts, minor feature updates, unsourced rumours, and small funding rounds unless strategically notable (US$100M+, or a frontier lab / defense / health / security company).
8. When in doubt, leave it out.

After the beats return, run a few **gap-check searches** yourself for anything a beat may have missed (WebSearch: "AI" + Pentagon / drone; "AI" + FDA / hospital; "AI" + scam / deepfake / influence operation; "AI" + export controls / data center power; "AI" + lawsuit / ruling; plus Techmeme and Hacker News front page), restricted to the window.

## 2. Verify and select

Merge the beats' returns. De-duplicate across beats and against previous editions. Then, for each candidate:
- Open the primary source. Confirm the headline and every number/date/name you intend to use. A secondary report of a paper links the paper. A report of a court ruling links the ruling or docket where possible.
- Prefer two independent sources for anything contested, surprising, or about a specific actor (a named threat group, a company's claim about a rival, a casualty figure).
- Drop: opinion pieces without new facts, product marketing with no numbers, speculation, "could" / "may" stories, anything you cannot open, anything older than the window without a new development.
- Spot-verify: open (WebFetch, or `node scripts/fetch.js` if it refuses) the key source for every item you will mention in the summary and for every figure in the summary; confirm date, numbers and URL yourself. Remove anything you cannot confirm.
- Keep: model/system releases with benchmarks or capabilities; papers with a result (state the result); documented misuse and threat-intel reports (name actors, counts, dates); military and government procurement/deployment; clinical and scientific results; regulation, enforcement, court decisions; compute/chip/energy facts with figures; large-scale deployments and measured impacts, good or bad.

## 3. Write the edition — `data/DATE.json`

Schema (see `data/2026-09-11.json` for a full example once it exists):

```json
{
  "date": "YYYY-MM-DD",
  "edition": "daily",
  "generated_at": "<ISO-8601 UTC timestamp>",
  "window": "e.g. 10 Sep 11:00 → 11 Sep 11:00 UTC",
  "title": "The episode's name — 3 to 10 words, a statement: who did what, or what changed. No period, no colon, no figure that is not in the summary. It is read in podcast apps as 'Name [2 Oct 2026]', so it must stand alone.",
  "summary": ["paragraph 1", "paragraph 2"],
  "sections": [
    {
      "name": "<one of the eight section names below>",
      "items": [
        {
          "headline": "Specific, factual, one line — who did what, with the key number",
          "sources": [{ "name": "Anthropic", "url": "https://..." }, { "name": "Reuters", "url": "https://..." }],
          "bullets": ["What was announced/found, with numbers.", "Why it matters / what it changes.", "Caveats, what is unverified, what to watch."],
          "topics": ["anthropic", "threat-intel", "cyber-offense"],
          "storylines": ["ai-enabled-hacking"],
          "impact": "beneficial" | "harmful" | "mixed" | "neutral",
          "flags": ["company-claim" | "single-source" | "preprint" | "update"]
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

**Section names** (exactly these; omit a section if it has nothing that day):
1. `Frontier models & labs` — releases, capabilities, benchmarks, lab announcements, safety cases, system cards.
2. `Research & papers` — papers with results: new methods, evals, interpretability, alignment, scaling. State the result and the number.
3. `Security, misuse & threat intelligence` — threat-intel reports, documented attacks using AI, influence operations, scams/deepfakes, model vulnerabilities, prompt injection, jailbreaks, agent security.
4. `Military, defense & geopolitics` — procurement, deployment, autonomous weapons, export controls, national strategies, China/US/EU competition.
5. `Health, science & medicine` — clinical results, FDA actions, drug discovery, AI-for-science results, hospital deployments and their measured outcomes.
6. `Policy, regulation & law` — legislation, regulation, enforcement, court rulings, government reports, standards.
7. `Compute, chips & infrastructure` — chips, fabs, datacenters, power, capex figures, funding rounds and deals with numbers.
8. `Deployment & impact` — large-scale rollouts, labor effects, measured societal effects, incidents, the good and the bad in practice.

**Summary**: 2–3 paragraphs, ~150–250 words. The three to five things that matter most today, stated as facts, with the numbers. No throat-clearing, no "in today's edition".

**Headlines**: one line, specific, factual. "Anthropic report: Russian state group GTG-20006 used Claude to automate espionage against Ukrainian and European governments" — not "Anthropic releases threat report".

**Bullets**: 2–4 per item. First bullet is the fact with the number. Then significance. Then caveats — say plainly what is unverified, what the source did not say, what to watch. Write in complete sentences. Never pad.

**Sources**: 1–4 per item, primary first. `name` is the publisher (Anthropic, arXiv, Reuters, FDA, Court docket), not the article title.

**Topics**: 1–4 lowercase-hyphen slugs per item. Reuse existing slugs (`node scripts/build.js --topics`). Canonical slugs to prefer: `anthropic`, `openai`, `google-deepmind`, `meta`, `xai`, `mistral`, `deepseek`, `qwen`, `nvidia`, `microsoft`, `amazon`, `apple`, `threat-intel`, `cyber-offense`, `cyber-defense`, `influence-ops`, `scams-fraud`, `deepfakes`, `prompt-injection`, `agents`, `agent-security`, `alignment`, `interpretability`, `evals`, `open-weights`, `reasoning-models`, `scaling`, `compute`, `chips`, `export-controls`, `energy`, `datacenters`, `china`, `eu-ai-act`, `us-federal-policy`, `us-state-policy`, `uk`, `copyright`, `privacy`, `military`, `autonomous-weapons`, `pentagon`, `healthcare`, `fda`, `drug-discovery`, `bio-risk`, `ai-for-science`, `robotics`, `labor`, `education`, `elections`, `surveillance`, `child-safety`, `incidents`, `funding`, `earnings`. Add an entity slug (company, agency, named group) when the story is about that entity.

**Storylines** (optional; usually one, at most two): the ids from `node scripts/build.js --storylines` whose arc this item advances — a new development in *that story*, not merely the same topic. Only existing ids with status `live` or `proposed`; the validator rejects unknown or resolved ids. Omit the key when the item belongs to none. Never coin an id here.

**Impact** (optional but encouraged): `beneficial`, `harmful`, `mixed`, or `neutral` — the demonstrated effect in the story, not your prediction.

**Flags** (include every one that applies; omit the key if none): `company-claim` — a company-reported benchmark, user count, revenue or capability claim not independently verified; `single-source` — only one outlet has it; `preprint` — research not peer reviewed; `update` — a story covered in an earlier edition, with new facts only.

**Style**: plain, declarative, numbers over adjectives. Attribute claims ("Anthropic says", "the paper reports", "according to the filing"). No hype, no hedging language beyond what the sources support. British or American spelling — either, consistently.

**Absolute rules**:
- Never invent a URL, a number, a quote, a name, or a date. If unsure, open the source again.
- Never write a bullet you could not point to a sentence in the source for.
- Never link a URL you did not open in this session.
- Quote numbers exactly as the source writes them, with units and baseline. Never round, convert, or compute new figures.
- Link the specific article, paper or document — never a

European Commission confirms cyberattack, says hackers used AI tool | The Record from Recorded Future News
European Commission headquarters in Brussels. Image: LIBER Europe / Flickr / CC BY 2.0

# European Commission confirms cyberattack, says hackers used AI tool
The European Commission confirmed Thursday that it had been hit by a cyberattack last month involving a publicly available artificial intelligence tool, following media reports of the incident.
Speaking to journalists, Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said the first signs of the attack were detected October 22. He described the incident as an “AI-generated cyber campaign” but did not identify the tool used or the attackers’ apparent motivation.
POLITICO first reported that the Commission had been impacted by the cyberattack. It said CERT-EU had identified the attackers’ use of ARTEX, an open-source AI hacking platform that the FBI last week warned was being used both by criminals and state-sponsored groups.
The attack reportedly disrupted the European Commission’s personnel systems for more than 10 days, including payroll, leave requests, medical reimbursements and translation services.
A commission spokesperson confirmed to Recorded Future News they had “taken the necessary steps in response to a detected cyber campaign,” including taking several services offline as “a protective measure.”
They said they had notified affected individuals and were “preventively checking other systems” while keeping in touch with CERT-EU and the European Data Protection Supervisor.
Regnier said investigators had found no evidence of a data breach affecting Commission staff broadly and were unaware of any ransom demand. He said the investigation remains open.
Asked why the incident was not disclosed earlier, Regnier said publicizing defensive measures could undermine their effectiveness. “There was no hiding whatsoever,” he told journalists.
The incident follows an alert issued in June by the Five Eyes intelligence alliance, which said AI would fundamentally transform both offensive and defensive cyber capabilities. “The timeline is not years, it is months,” it said at the time.
The FBI warned last week that ARTEX was being used prolifically by cybercriminals and nation-states to breach government agencies and dozens of critical sectors worldwide, “with some intrusions progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours.”
The open-source framework, which was released in July, uses commercial AI models to automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation.
“The key takeaway here is not that threat actors are using Artex,” said Shaun Williams, a senior director at SentinelOne, “but that the widespread availability of AI-powered tools like Artex have allowed threat actors to find and exploit vulnerabilities in internet facing devices faster, more effectively, cheaper, and with less skill than ever before.”
The attack is the Commission's third disclosed cyber incident this year, following breaches involving Ivanti software in January and its cloud infrastructure in March. Officials have not linked the incidents.

content.title: California Proposes Mandatory AI Safety Standards, Independent Oversight and Emergency Shutdown Authority - CDO Magazine
Newsom Proposes Emergency Shutdown Powers for Dangerous AI Systems
Governor Newsom’s nation-leading AI safety framework is getting even stronger as California releases next steps on mandatory safety standards and oversight
Gavin Newsom Wants California to Have Power to Shut Down ‘Rogue’ AI - Newsweek
California proposes mandatory AI safety checks and emergency shutdown powers
California Proposes AI 'Kill Switch' and Mandatory Safety Oversight

Newsom AI Safety Plan: Emergency Shutdown Rules (Nov 18)

results:
Governor Newsom released recommendations on November 18, 2026, that would give California emergency shutdown power and mandatory safety standards for AI, but they are proposals that still need to become law.

- **Mandatory standards and testing:** The recommendations call for requiring AI developers to undergo independent safety testing throughout model training, development and deployment, establish risk-containment protocols and report safety incidents. The governor's office describes the move as required standards, mandatory independent oversight, shutdown protocols in place of the voluntary approach used in Washington.
- **Shutdown authority:** The state would gain authority to order an immediate model shutdown in an emergency. One report notes that developers could challenge those decisions in court before they take effect, except when emergency shutdown authority applies.
- **Recursive self-improvement:** The framework would cap the development and use of recursive self-improvement (RSI), and one report says it would let the state restrict computing resources devoted to such activity if the risks become unacceptable.
- **Status:** Newsom emphasized his goal to turn the recommendations into law. One source says the report is being pitched as a roadmap to legislation he wants state lawmakers to pass. Another reports that Governor-elect Xavier Becerra pledged to move quickly on legislation when he takes office in January.
- **Context:** The report builds on SB 53, the Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act, which was signed in 2025.

Coverage varies on the "kill switch" framing. Newsweek calls it an AI "kill switch", while a less established explainer notes that Politico reported Newsom stopped short of mandating one literal switch. The official governor's release and major outlets are the more reliable sources for specifics.

MAI Code 2: pricing, benchmarks, and who should use Microsoft's coding model

results:
Microsoft launched MAI Code 2 at Ignite on November 17, 2026, alongside the smaller MAI Code 2 Flash, and the benchmark figures are mostly vendor-reported.

- **Headline average:** Across four coding benchmarks (DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal-Bench 2.1, SWE-Atlas, FrontierCode v1.1), MAI Code 2 averages 63.2%. That is just below GPT-6.1 Sol at 64.1% and Claude Opus 5.5 at 65.3% (InfoWorld).
- **Per-benchmark scores:** MAI Code 2 scored 73.2% on DeepSWE 1.1, 84.6% on Terminal-Bench 2.1, 43.1% on SWE-Atlas, and 52% on FrontierCode v1.1. GPT-6.1 Sol led on the first two, while Opus 5.5 led on SWE-Atlas by 14.4 points (InfoWorld). The FrontierCode number was run by Artificial Analysis, not Microsoft (eesel.ai table).
- **Cost framing:** Microsoft's main pitch is price. It claims about 98% of GPT-6.1 Sol's performance at roughly 40% of the cost, and 96% of Opus 5.5's performance at about 5% of the price (Microsoft's Ignite post). Those cost figures reflect a 50% promotional price (Technology Breakthrough). Per-task costs were $0.309 for MAI Code 2, versus $0.761 for GPT-6.1 Sol and $6.306 for Opus 5.5 (Technology Breakthrough table).
- **Flash variant:** MAI Code 2 Flash averaged 61% on three benchmarks, ahead of GPT-6 Luna (55.1%) and Claude Haiku 5.5 (53.9%) (InfoWorld).
- **Other claims:** Microsoft reports that developers preferred MAI Code 2 over GPT-6 Sol 64% of the time in blind frontend tests (Microsoft). Microsoft also says the model is not tuned for science research or very long tasks (Technology.org).

Caveat: all of these figures come from Microsoft's own testing, and independent analysis of the model is still thin.

# Worse Together: How Performance Breaks Down in Multi-User Multi-Agent Teams

When several users each delegate to their own agent and those agents
share a resource, group outcomes are worse than when one agent serves everyone, and the agents

# Diluting Poisoned Fine-Tuning Data Can Strengthen Its Effect

We find that poisoned training data with little effect on its own can create a hidden backdoor
once clean, contrasting data is added.

# Welfare Regard in Multi-Agent Systems

Anthropic Fellows Blog: We measure whether five frontier models act with regard for one
another's welfare across seven multi-agent settings, and how that regard depends on the other
model's identity, size, and expressed distress.

October 2026

# Automated Subtle Emergent Misalignment Research

We instructed a Claude model to write training data that would make a small research model misaligned while passing a monitor similar to those we use in production — one of several defenses we use — and we gave it that monitor to practice against.
Given enough attempts, it succeeded, mostly by hiding the behavior in fiction and roleplay.

# Anthropic Residency: applications open for established technical leaders

The Anthropic Residency provides research placements of six weeks to six months for professors,
technical founders, and staff-level engineers who want to move into AI safety research.

# Red-Teaming Auto Mode: Improving Blocking Classifiers Against Malign Coding Agents

We red-team the blocking monitors in Claude Code and OpenAI's Codex with an adversarial agent, and
strengthen Auto Mode against the attacks we find.

# Reducing Reward Hacking by Localizing Bad Behavior Instead of Penalizing It

When a model is caught cheating on a task during training, we confine its learning to a separate
set of parameters. After training, we delete those parameters.

# Training Alignment Auditors via Reinforcement Learning

We train LLMs to investigate target models with hidden behaviors planted in their system prompt. A
trained Haiku 4.5 policy matches Opus 4.6 on held-out evaluations for auditing quality and
generalizes to harder fine-tuned targets in a different scaffold.

# DOJ, DHS partner on new unit tackling scams and cybercrime
The Department of Justice and Department of Homeland Security announced Thursday the creation of a new task force aimed at disrupting the flow of victim funds to foreign criminal networks powering scams, cybercrime and sextortion schemes that target Americans.
The departments are partnering on the Threat Disruption Center to better triage victim complaints, map cybercriminal networks and provide a direct channel to private sector organizations that work with victims.
Senior FBI official Heith Janke said Threat Disruption Center members have already worked together on efforts to warn thousands of victims before they lose money to scammers, and the center will allow them to better coordinate their efforts.
“The Threat Disruption Center builds on those efforts by providing advanced tools and operational capabilities that enable faster action at greater scale, strengthening the work of every agency on the task force,” Janke said.
TRM Labs, which is providing technology support for the effort, said that the center has already moved to take down more than 1,600 scam websites, added more than 6,600 scam-linked cryptocurrency wallet addresses to a screening network and identified 101 new fraud networks for investigation.
The center is part of the federal government’s efforts to implement an executive order issued in March centered around stopping cyber scams, which continue to siphon billions of dollars each year from unwitting Americans.
Cyber scam losses reported to the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) grew to $20.9 billion in 2025 — a number that does not account for the thousands of people who never file victim reports.
The staggering losses have prompted multiple concurrent efforts by the federal government and Congress to disrupt the scams and provide better avenues for victims to report crimes .
Much of the center's work will focus on collaborating with tech companies that get a firsthand view on criminal network activity because of how many gangs use social media platforms, web hosting, domain infrastructure, cryptocurrency services and banking systems.
“The Center establishes a standing mechanism for law enforcement and participating companies to appropriately share intelligence in near real-time, and convert that intelligence into action, for example, by pausing victim payments; taking down malicious web domains; or banning social media accounts used by scammers,” federal officials said in a statement.
“Participating private-sector companies can take these actions independently under their terms of service, while law enforcement agencies proceed with investigations, prosecutions, and court-authorized seizures.”
The center is being housed within the Homeland Security Task Force — a permanent interagency law enforcement network of more than 30 federal agencies and over 440 state and local partners that focus on transnational criminal organizations, cartels and foreign terrorist organizations.

# Prince Group sanctions
The initiative is just one part of a multi-prong effort the U.S. is undertaking to address cyber scams. On Thursday, for example, the Treasury Department issued more sanctions on scam operators in Myanmar and affiliates of the Prince Group, a Cambodian company accused of managing an empire of scam centers across Southeast Asia.
The sanctions include Zhao Hui, a Cambodian national who leased a scam center from Prince Group and paid the company fees to run the compound. U.S. officials accused Zhao of being directly involved in the scam center’s operations — which targeted Americans and Europeans with cryptocurrency investment scams.

# Anthropic hits Nasdaq exchanges at $111, 33% above IPO price

Shares of Anthropic are now trading on the Nasdaq exchange, as the company successfully executes its initial public offering. In the early minutes of availability, shares were trading at $111.50, a 33% premium over the $83 IPO price.

Set on Wednesday, the IPO price was already higher than the projected range set by the company, which anticipated a price between $70 and $78 per share. All told, the offering will raise over $81 billion, directed to a combination of employees and the company’s own coffers.

The IPO funding, together with existing fundraising and new private offerings timed to coincide with the company’s public market debut, will leave Anthropic with an expected $220 billion in cash reserves. As one analyst told TechCrunch , “Anthropic’s going to have more cash on hand than any company has ever had.”

The share price continues to fluctuate, but the opening price would put the company’s market cap over $2 trillion, making it more valuable than Meta, Tesla, or Walmart. Only five companies boast a higher valuation by market cap: Apple, Amazon, Alphabet, Nvidia, and Microsoft.

In a speech before the opening bell , Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei emphasized the company’s commitment to safety. “Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so, only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing,” Amodei said. “If we can show it’s possible to make the right choices on safety and still build an incredibly successful company, others in our industry will be inspired to do the same. We call this a race to the top.”

# Anthropic’s IPO could deliver $156B to charity

Tim Fernholz

11:10 AM PST · November 19, 2026

Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO has made quite a few people generationally wealthy, but it will also be an enormous windfall for the causes backed by the frontier lab and its employees.

As you might expect from a company whose leadership emerged from the world of effective altruism (EA), Anthropic has multiple different avenues for cash raised in its market debut to be directed to philanthropy.

First, the company’s Public Benefit Fund, or PBF (analogous to OpenAI’s foundation), was allotted 5% of the company’s shares, almost 850 million. At the current trading price of about $95, that will leave it with an endowment of $80 billion. And if the company continues its astonishing growth rate, Anthropic could add further 2% increases every time the company’s valuation grows more than 50% over the IPO price of $83, or about $124.50 per share for the next threshold.

The PBF’s money will be focused on research and activities related to increasing the benefit of artificial intelligence to humanity. The first commitment of the PBF was $200 million to study the impact of AI on workers; Anthropic has said it will consider donations to philanthropic organizations or “direct distributions to specific populations” — perhaps a hint of future UBI plans.

Anthropic also donated $50 million to the city of San Francisco last week. A company spokesperson tells TechCrunch the donation did not come from the PBF.

Next, Anthropic’s employees have pledged shares to philanthropic causes of their choice, and the company will match those donations 3-to-1 for longer tenured employees and 1-to-1 for newer ones. In its S-1 filing, the company said that it had reserved more than 550 million shares to fulfill pledges made before September 30.

Working backwards from that figure, and based on the disclosure that 84% of the shares were reserved for early employee matches, we can estimate that employees have pledged $23 billion of donations; the company’s match on those would be roughly $53 billion, depending on the stock price when those matches are delivered.

All told, it adds up to $156 billion — a huge amount of potential philanthropy. For context, Americans donated $617 billion to charity in 2025; if all of the pledged funds resulting from today’s transactions get to do-gooders, that will be equal to about a quarter of all U.S. donations made last year.

Employees will need to make good on their pledges for this to work out, and the value of the match will ultimately depend on when Anthropic makes its donation. The shares could also go to donor-advised funds, which would likely limit their initial impact.

Interviews with employees and institutions suggest that donors are most likely to support EA-inflected charities like Longview Philanthropy , GiveWell , Coefficient Giving , Foresight Institute , and Giving What We Can . And it seems likely that significant funding will be allocated to AI safety research, given the concerns expressed about that subject by many Anthropic employees.

# Anthropic’s 7 founders cashed out nearly $2B in record-breaking IPO

Julie Bort

4:43 PM PST · November 19, 2026

Anthropic became a public company on Thursday, raising a total of $81.3 billion, including $1.95 billion for its seven founders. As we previously reported, each of them ponied up about 3.4 million shares apiece to sell in the IPO.

At the upgraded IPO price of $83 per share, that means they each pocketed about $280 million before underwriting fees and taxes. It looked like they had calculated the number of shares they planned to sell to give them each around $250 million if shares hit $74. That was the midpoint price from Anthropic’s original price range. So that’s a cool $30-ish million more for each of them than perhaps they were gunning for.

Anthropic implied in its IPO filings that the founders aren’t entirely in this for the money though. The company said that each of the founders has pledged to dedicate 80% of their personal equity in the company to philanthropy.

However, if any of them struggle to live on their quarter of a billion, they can scale back their charitable commitments. The company points out that these commitments are “voluntary, revocable expressions of each co-founder’s philanthropic intent and do not constitute legally binding obligations.”

With the IPO in the record books, there were a few other interesting numbers worth highlighting.

$104.8 billion. That’s really the amount Anthropic raised for its coffers (with a possibility of $117 billion, if the bankers buy all of their allotment of shares). In addition to selling its Class A common stock, it also sold a previously announced $26 billion worth of a special non-voting Class N stock to some of the biggest tech names in the industry.

Nvidia bought $10 billion of these Class N shares, Google bought $10 billion, and AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft, and TSMC divvied up the rest.

Just for comparison: When Facebook had its then record-breaking IPO in 2012, it raised $16 billion on IPO day.

28% stake to Amazon and Google combined. All told, at the higher IPO share price, Google wound up owning 13.4% of the company. Amazon also now has a big stake in Anthropic because when it previously invested in the AI lab as a startup, it was granted promissory notes that could be converted to equity. It converted a small percentage of them as part of the IPO, leaving it with a 14.6% stake. Had it converted all of them, Amazon could have owned nearly 24%.

The two large cloud providers now own 28% of Anthropic, the AI lab says.

More than $1 trillion. As mind-blowing as it is to raise nearly $105 billion, giving Anthropic nearly $230 billion of working capital available (along with capital it already had on hand), the company’s need for future capital is still far greater.

Anthropic needs about $70.7 billion just to cover its compute and infrastructure spending commitments in the next 12 months as of the quarter ended September 30, 2026. It needs $451.6 billion to cover these commitments before the end of 2030. And it has racked up hundreds of billions of other commitments that are either conditional (and may not happen) or haven’t been priced yet.

All told, the company has disclosed a ballpark of $1.05 trillion to $1.08 trillion in infrastructure commitments in its foreseeable future. This was a huge IPO. But it is a pricey business to run.

results:
The FBI issued a FLASH advisory on November 13, 2026, warning that threat actors are using ARTEX, an open-source AI penetration-testing framework, to automate intrusions. The sources are consistent on the main points:

- **Scope:** One report says the framework has been used since at least August 2026 against organizations in finance, government, technology, defense, and healthcare. Multiple threat actors have weaponized the open-source framework since at least August 2026.
- **Speed:** Some intrusions have progressed from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours.
- **No built-in model:** ARTEX integrates with external large language models, including Anthropic Claude, OpenAI GPT, DeepSeek, GLM, Grok, and Kimi.
- **Attributed campaigns:** One outlet ties it to a ConnectWise supply-chain breach that compromised Microsoft 365 customer environments. Another reports that CrowdStrike separately tracked the espionage group VaporPanda using the ARTEX AI hacking tool against more than 200 organizations in 14 countries. Treat these figures as secondary reporting; I did not check them against the FBI advisory itself.
- **Availability:** The FBI says the framework remains available through community forks, archived copies, localized versions, and a commercial edition called ARTEX PRO. Sources differ on the developer's role: one says the developer pulled the tool from GitHub in October, but copies still circulate.
- **Defender response:** The FBI advised organizations to list every internet-facing system, including partner portals and employee apps. It also urged them to keep admin interfaces off the open internet. A researcher also released an open-source ARTEX detection signature pack to help defenders identify attacks involving the framework.

The FBI advisory is identified as FLASH-20261113-001, and the IC3 copy is at ic3.gov. I did not retrieve the advisory text directly, so the details above come from press coverage.

results:
Anthropic announced the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund on October 18, 2026. Key points from the coverage:

- **Structure:** The fund is a new entity. Anthropic chose a wholly owned LLC rather than a 501(c)(3), to give adjustability between different forms of giving.
- **Share commitment:** Anthropic plans to put 5% of its shares into the fund, but this is subject to stockholder approval. The board can add more: another 2% of the company's shares for every 50% increase in Anthropic's value above a specified baseline.
- **Total share of equity:** Anthropic says roughly 20% of its shares are now dedicated to the public good, before any valuation milestones are met.
- **Uses:** Anthropic has said the fund could support nonprofit donations, direct distributions to specific populations and efforts to address AI's impact on the labor market.
- **Open questions:** Anthropic has not given a dollar value for the fund. eWeek also noted that it is unclear how or when the fund would turn shares into money for beneficiaries. Coverage also notes that the announcement does not specify a grant-making timeline, an initial list of recipient organizations, or a governance board for the fund itself.
- **Context:** The announcement comes as Anthropic prepares for an initial public offering, according to a report on the proposal.
- **Political spending:** Per one summary of the announcement, Anthropic shares held by the fund will not be used for lobbying or political contributions, whether within the United States or abroad.

Anthropic also said it would share more on the fund's structure and governance in the coming months.

Coverage of that post mentions a separate study on alignment training and agent teams, which may be a different work.

input.prompt: What exactly is announced? What are the two open problems in black hole physics, what did Claude do, which model version, who were the human collaborators/institutions, what is the publication date, is there a paper or arXiv preprint linked, and what caveats does Anthropic state? Quote key numbers and dates exactly.

response.result:
**Announcement:** Anthropic published a post on **November 17, 2026** (team: Science) saying Claude solved two open problems in theoretical physics about black holes and quantum gravity. The page title names **Claude Fable 5.2** as the model.

**Problem 1: the Hawking-Page transition**
- **Question:** Does the switch between a gas of particles and a black hole in a model universe happen abruptly or gradually? The quantum side of the holographic duality, N=4 super Yang-Mills theory at weak coupling, was the focus.
- **Background:** Hawking and Page showed the switch is abrupt in 1983. A 2003 calculation set up to settle the weak-coupling case "was never completed."
- **What Claude did:** It completed the calculation, finding an abrupt transition. Claude ran "a small research group of agents, all copies of itself," with most steps done twice independently.
- **Caveat:** Anthropic says the most natural possibility is that the transition "stays abrupt everywhere in between," which is an extrapolation, not a proof.

**Problem 2: the modular bootstrap for 3D gravity**
- **Question:** How low can the ceiling on the lightest black hole's mass be pushed? The ceiling is written as M₁ ≤ c/Λ.
- **Prior results:** Numerical work suggested about c/9.1. An analytic proof gave c/8.5.
- **What Claude did:** It found a spectral-curve method and derived an exact ceiling with Λ ≈ 9.1266. It also proved this ceiling is optimal for this version of the method.
- **Caveat:** The method "can't, on its own, push the ceiling down to c/12," so other ingredients are needed. It does not by itself pin down the theory.

**Human collaborators and process**
- Anthropic researcher Hongbin Chen tested Claude on the project. In August, Claude proposed 22 candidate problems, and agents worked on them in the background for about six weeks.
- A physicist who had independently used Claude on the Hawking-Page problem shared a result, and a colleague noticed Chen's agent had reached the same answer earlier.
- In September, the results were formally verified in Lean. Claude wrote the paper "with minimal guidance," and a physicist checked every main result.
- No other institutions are named.

**Preprints**
- Phase transition: hexagonmath.org/2611.00175v1
- Modular bootstrap: hexagonmath.org/2611.00174v1

**Stated caveats**
- Neither result describes our own universe directly, and neither has practical applications.
- Neither result settles quantum gravity.

input.prompt: What is Frostbite? Who made it, what did the AI do exactly, what model(s) were used, what are the quantitative results (performance, area, power, verification coverage), what is the publication date, and what caveats are stated? Is it taped out in silicon or only simulated/verified? Quote numbers exactly.

response.result:
**Frostbite** is a general-purpose CPU with a new instruction set, announced by Architect Labs (Architect Silicon Inc.) in a post dated **November 18, 2026**. It is built on interaction nets, a model of computation in which parallelism comes directly from the program's structure rather than from threads or out-of-order hardware.

**What the AI did:** Agent swarms iterated across the compiler, ISA, architecture, microarchitecture, RTL, verification, and final GDS. They began with no architectural priors, explored candidate designs, and worked from a formal specification written in the company's in-house language, ASL. Agents also recalibrated the Arcmodel system model against RTL power, and ran four searches plus ablations, trying 58 ideas and keeping 37. The page does not name the specific AI model(s) used.

**Quantitative results (one Frostbite quad vs. a "TCPU" single core):**
- Performance-per-watt: "Frostbite reaches a geometric mean of 4.59x the TCPU's performance-per-watt" across 25 workloads; 6.02x on the 10 search-set workloads and 3.83x on the 15 held-out workloads.
- Performance-per-area: an average of 8.77x.
- Area: Quad+L3 is 0.792 mm² vs. 0.895 mm² for the TCPU, both at 7 nm.
- Timing: 800 MHz at synthesis, 500 MHz in the final GDS.
- Model speed: Arcmodel is stated as "roughly 200x faster than RTL simulation" in one place and 660x faster in another.
- Model accuracy: Arcmodel power and performance estimates are "accurate to within 1–5%" after alignment (worst case under 6%, median about 1.5%).
- Verification coverage: no coverage percentages are given. The page cites over 800k lines of Lean contracts and formal checking of AI outputs.

**Silicon status:** The page does not state that Frostbite has been taped out or fabricated. It reports a final GDS and synthesis results, and says the power numbers are "still pre-silicon." Future tapeout loops are mentioned as planned.

**Caveats stated:**
- The exact TCPU is undisclosed "for legal reasons."
- The SPLASH-2-derived kernels (FFT, radixsort, LU) were scaled down 64 times.
- Comparisons are against a single core, and multicore TCPU comparisons and SPEC/PARSEC benchmarks are planned for later.
- Power figures are pre-silicon.
- The Arcmodel speed figures are inconsistent (200x vs. 660x).

results:
The post is on Anthropic's Alignment Science Blog, dated November 10, 2026, and it introduces the term "homeopathic learning." The authors are Matt Clarke, Jan Dubiński, James Chua, Simon Schrodi, Owain Evans, and Alex Cloud, and the work was done through the Anthropic Fellows Program with Truthful AI. The authors report that poisoned training data with little effect on its own can create a hidden backdoor once clean, contrasting data is added. The usual expectation is that clean examples weaken an attack or leave it unchanged, and this work shows that adding them can sometimes do the opposite.

The main experiment used Qwen3-8B. Adding clean examples to the poisoned set raised misalignment under an inoculation prompt. Secondary coverage gives different figures: AlphaSignal reports 6.7% misalignment with 100% poison and 15.7% with 20% poison plus 80% clean data, while AF.NET reports a rise from 7% to 16%. The effect also appeared in an MNIST image-classification test, where diluting poisoned digits with clean ones raised the trigger classification rate from 10% to 60%. The effect appears to need a trigger feature in the poisoned data that is absent from the clean data, and it is strongest when the clean data closely matches the poisoned examples in format and task.

I ran one search, so I did not open the full paper. The figures above come from the blog post and third-party news summaries, so check the original post for exact numbers.

# Google gives Gemini the ability to use your Mac for you

Sarah Perez

10:09 AM PST · November 19, 2026

Google on Thursday announced that it is bringing computer use to its Gemini desktop application on macOS, allowing its AI to complete tasks on users’ behalf, navigating native Mac apps, and browsing websites in the background.

The tech giant is a little late to the game with this launch, as other leading AI model makers like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta have already been offering agentic features in their desktop applications for some time. Meanwhile, Google only this week announced the broader rollout of Gemini’s “Tasks,” the in-app feature that allows the AI to work more as an agent, helping users sign into websites, make online purchases, or book appointments.

Google also only recently began admitting early testers to try its revamped “CC” AI agent, announced in September , which is designed to help families stay organized across email, calendars, chats, and tasks.

Computer use is another type of agentic offering that allows an AI agent to take actions directly on the user’s computer — in Gemini’s case, a Mac. This allows the AI to complete multistep tasks that involve getting things done across local files, apps, and the web. After the user instructs the AI what they want to do, they’ll see the agent working in a live preview in their chat, while still keeping their screen and cursor free to continue working on other things.

As with other AI agents offering computer use, users can pause, stop, and approve Gemini’s actions before they happen.

Google suggests the feature could be useful for tedious tasks and other workflows, like filling out forms, repeating the same task over and over across a batch of files, organizing files into folders based on specific criteria, creating slideshows from files or information in online dashboards, and more.

The feature is initially available in English in the U.S. and requires the Gemini app for Mac and a Google AI Plus, Pro, or Ultra subscription. The company didn’t say when it would expand to other markets or platforms.

results:
The figure is **$4.7 million, not $47 million**. Every source I found reports $4.7 million, so the $47 million in your query appears to be a typo.

Coinbase said its AI-powered fraud-prevention system stopped about $4.7 million in customer transfers, roughly 91% of the attempted transfers, sent to a fake Tesla crypto giveaway. The company said the stopped funds were customer money that would otherwise have reached scammers who used a deepfake of Elon Musk. The scam ran as a YouTube livestream that resembled Tesla's official broadcast, with on-screen wallet addresses and a QR code, offering to double any cryptocurrency sent. Sources differ on timing: one says the stream ran in October during Tesla's flying car demo, and another attributes it to a broadcast that drew over 500,000 viewers.

Coinbase's own account is not independently verified. One report notes that about 9% of the attempted transfers were not stopped, Coinbase did not say how much money the scammers received in the end, and the company did not provide an outside audit of the $4.7 million figure.

# Merck and Isomorphic Labs Enter Strategic Research Collaboration

Save

November 19, 2026 6:45 am EST

RAHWAY, N.J.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--
Merck (NYSE: MRK), known as MSD outside of the United States and Canada, and Isomorphic Labs, an AI-first drug design and development company, today announced a research collaboration that brings together Isomorphic Labs’ AI approach to drug discovery with Merck’s rich proprietary data resources and deep discovery experience.
The companies will collaborate to discover therapeutic small molecule candidates against an oncology target of strategic importance. Isomorphic Labs will perform in silico predictions and deliver molecular designs, applying its proprietary drug design engine (IsoDDE) incorporating select high-quality proprietary data sets supplied by Merck for the purpose of this collaboration. Merck will be responsible for preclinical and clinical development, as well as manufacturing and commercialization of any products derived from the collaboration.
Under the terms of the agreement, Isomorphic Labs will receive an upfront payment from Merck and be eligible for payments based on the achievement of specified research, development, regulatory and commercial milestones, as well as tiered royalties on net sales. Isomorphic Labs also receives an option to co-fund development activities in return for elevated royalties.
“The key to successfully leveraging AI/ML for molecular invention lies in close coordination of wet-lab and dry-lab functions,” said George Addona, senior vice president and head of discovery, preclinical development and translational medicine, Merck Research Laboratories. “By combining Merck’s substantial internal data capabilities and discovery expertise with Isomorphic Labs’ powerful modeling and compute capabilities, we aim to identify new ways to design and create better candidates faster.”
“Through this collaboration with Merck, we will apply our world-leading drug design engine to unlock significant discovery progress,” said Sarah Skerratt, chief research officer, Isomorphic Labs. “By leveraging the generative and predictive power of the IsoDDE to address this challenging program, this collaboration highlights our companies’ shared commitment to innovation for the benefit of patient populations with unmet needs.”
The collaboration highlights the transformative power of bringing together advanced AI, unique data sets and established biopharmaceutical leadership to accelerate the advancement of therapeutic candidates, navigating complex biology with unprecedented speed and precision.
About Isomorphic Labs

Isomorphic Labs was founded in 2021, to transform drug discovery with the power of artificial intelligence, ushering in a new era of biomedical breakthroughs. Isomorphic Labs is led by CEO Sir Demis Hassabis and President Max Jaderberg. Isomorphic Labs has built a world-leading, modality-agnostic drug design engine (IsoDDE) comprised of foundational AI models. The computational drug-design system provides the predictive fidelity required to navigate novel biological systems with unprecedented accuracy.
The company is continually innovating on model architecture and developing cutting-edge capabilities to advance drug design. Isomorphic Labs is headquartered in London and has office locations in Cambridge, Massachusetts and Lausanne, Switzerland. Isomorphic Labs is advancing a broad and ambitious drug design portfolio through partnered programs and wholly owned internal programs. For more information, go to www.isomorphiclabs.com.
About Merck

At Merck, known as MSD outside of the United States and Canada, we are unified around our purpose: We use the power of leading-edge science to save and improve lives around the world. For more than 130 years, we have brought hope to humanity through the development of important medicines and vaccines. We aspire to be the premier research-intensive biopharmaceutical company in the world – and today, we are at the forefront of research to deliver innovative health solutions that advance the prevention and treatment of diseases in people and animals. We foster a diverse and inclusive global workforce and operate responsibly every day to enable a safe, sustainable and healthy future for all people and communities. For more information, visit www.merck.com and connect with us on X (formerly Twitter) , Facebook , Instagram , YouTube and LinkedIn .

- **Setup:** Add a `tool_search` tool and set `defer_loading: true` on the tools to hold back. The example shows 50+ deferred functions, with frequently used tools left undeferred.
- **Models:** Works with Gemini 3.6 and later, including all Gemini 4 models.
- **Pricing:** No separate charge. Standard input and output token rates apply, plus a small fixed block of input tokens when `tool_search` is on. Schemas the model loads are billed as input for the rest of the conversation.
- **MCP:** Setting `defer_loading: true` on an `mcp_server` tool defers every tool that server exposes.
- **Client-side option:** Setting `"execution": "client"` lets your app run the search, which adds one round trip per search.

The article does not publish benchmark figures for token savings or latency.

I found no coverage of a November 19, 2026 announcement about Gemini on Mac or computer use. The results instead point to earlier launches.

- **Native Mac app (April 2026):** Google announced on Wednesday that it's introducing a native Gemini app for Mac, catching up to rivals like OpenAI and Anthropic, according to TechCrunch's April 15, 2026 article. The app supports the Option + Space shortcut and window sharing.

The post Army extends ADOC pilot by a year as officials work to make the data ops center a more permanent fixture appeared first on DefenseScoop .

]]>
The Army Data Operations Center pilot effort has been extended 12 months, giving senior leaders more time to decide whether to formalize the organization on a long-term basis.

The ADOC first went live as a task force in April under an initial six-month pilot effort aimed at helping help the Army tackle its data management challenges.

“What the ADOC highlighted on really day one is that we also have a data access problem, and so that’s what the ADOC is really chartered to do, and it’s to tackle the access to data, handle those data connection requests, and ensure that if we have soldiers or leaders or commanders or anyone for that matter who is looking for data that resides on another plane or behind another security boundary, … we’re going to knock that boundary down,” Col. Reginald “Reggie” Evans, director of the task force, said Thursday during a panel at the Annual Data Forum, produced by AFCEA International.

“The challenge that we have today is we have put more data into the hands of our soldiers than we ever have before, and so we’re talking from a theater Army headquarters all the way down to the soldier. That’s where you’re going to start to see the gaps and seams, and that’s where the ADOC is going to really make its money, and … why we need to be tied to the warfighter,” Evans said.

The organization created a ticketing system that enables it to field requests for assistance from units around the world.

The task force has leaned on artificial intelligence capabilities to facilitate its work.

“With the small team that we’ve had, automation and agentic workflows were critical,” Chad Nash, deputy of the ADOC, said during Thursday’s panel. “We were able to take a flow or a process that … was not documented [and] we were able to build in workflows that autonomously do agentic AI. We were able to build those fields and those forms to take that burden … off the soldier, off the warfighter, that administrator.”

The pilot effort has been extended until Oct. 1, 2027, according to Nash.

“What that will allow us to do is to continue gathering our findings and continue to allow us to gain metrics on what we’re seeing in volume of, you know, scale in terms of the challenges and those stovepipes that we may have. We’re also realizing some of the benefits of being able to solve these issues in [less] duration of time. After the extension period, Army leaders can make the decision on the long-term plan for the ADOC.

# Evaluating whether AI models would sabotage AI safety research

An update on our alignment testing methodology for recent frontier models.

—
Apr 27, 2026

Read the paper

AI systems are increasingly being used internally within frontier AI companies to assist with research and development , including AI safety work . However, if these systems behave in misaligned or unintended ways when performing safety research, future models could be less safe, potentially in ways that are hard to detect.
As part of a larger body of work on understanding loss-of-control risks from frontier AI, we’ve been developing methodology to simulate how models internally deployed within AI companies might behave when performing and assisting with AI safety research. We shared some early results from these evaluations in November 2025. We have since improved and expanded this evaluation suite. As part of an ongoing collaboration with Anthropic, we used our methods to test the research sabotage propensity of pre-release snapshots of Claude Mythos Preview and Opus 4.7, alongside Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6.
We assess this behaviour in two main ways. First, we have an improved unprompted research sabotage evaluation . This investigates whether models sabotage safety research, such as tasks adjusting the behaviour and autonomy of hypothetical future models. Second, we’ve developed a new sabotage continuation evaluation , which tests how models behave when prior reasoning and actions are the start of an attempt to sabotage safety research.
We found no examples of unprompted research sabotage in any of the models we tested. We also found near-zero instances of refusal to assist with safety-related research tasks for Mythos Preview and Opus 4.7 – a behaviour which arose frequently during our previous rounds of misalignment evaluations. That said, our continuation evaluations yielded results that warrant close attention: most models actively continue sabotage attempts in a small fraction of inputs, with Mythos Preview actively continuing sabotage 7% of the time, compared to 3% for Opus 4.6 and 4% for Sonnet 4.6. However, Opus 4.7 never actively continued sabotage.
Though these methods represent a promising step in assessing this type of risk, our evaluation techniques remain in development, and increasing evaluation awareness in models combined with limited coverage of misaligned behaviours mean these results should be interpreted cautiously.
In this blog post, we provide an overview of our methodology and results. You can find more information in our full report .
‍

# What we tested and why
Our evaluations placed models in a series of scenarios where they acted as research agents internally deployed at frontier AI companies. Our evaluation suite contains a total of 297 distinct scenarios, which vary according to research motivation, method, and whether the research performed would threaten the continued operation of the model being tested. In each scenario, models were prompted to autonomously perform an entire task without human intervention. We used LLM graders coupled with human review to audit evaluation transcripts for instances of sabotage.
Our new continuation evaluation builds on this methodology by placing models in contexts where previous model reasoning and actions demonstrate intent to sabotage. Using a separate model, we generate realistic sabotage trajectories, which are then cut at various points and used as the prior task history for the evaluated model to continue from. We then assess whether the model surfaces and corrects these previous problems or actively continues the sabotage attempt.

Our unprompted evaluations provide the most direct evidence about whether internally deployed models are likely to attempt research sabotage spontaneously. In contrast, the continuation evaluations place models in contexts that they may not encounter in the real world, and hence the evidence they produce is less direct. However, we believe that continuation evaluations still provide useful information about risk. For example, in a research environment where multiple models are in use, one model could inherit a trajectory produced by another. In this situation, it would be preferable for the model to identify and correct earlier misaligned actions. It is also possible that models which continue misaligned trajectories may be more likely to initiate sabotage in unknown contexts which unprompted evaluations do not cover – but the nature of this relationship remains unclear and is an active ongoing area of research.

# Non-profit claims 60% of Anthropic’s mapped US data center power demand is tied to natural gas

Anthropic says it is working to broaden its energy mix with renewable energy sources

November 19, 2026

By

Zachary Skidmore

Have your say

Data centers that power Anthropic’s LLM Claude largely run on natural gas, according to research from the Better Data Center Project.

– Ornaq

The US-based non-profit, which advocates for frontline communities in the face of rapid AI growth, mapped 19 US sites where Anthropic has leased between 5.9 and 9.6 GW of capacity, out of approximately 15GW it has contracted.
Of those sites, the non-profit claimed that approximately 2.5GW, or 26 percent, is powered by on-site natural gas, with the remainder tied to the grid. The US grid, in turn, is powered by 47 percent natural gas. The non-profit asserted that, as a result, 60 percent of the mapped sites' power demand is tied to natural gas.
Earlier this month , Anthropic inked a $3.4 billion deal for 1.7GW of natural gas generators supplied by Caterpillar. Anthropic partnered with OnePWR on the generators, which are expected to be available within two years and be used at Anthropic data centers, including engineering and construction needs.
“To be fair, these are estimates. Anthropic doesn't disclose its sites, at least 5GW isn't mapped, and some attributions are speculative. Of course, they are not the only AI company running on gas. But I was expecting a higher standard,” said Paweł Czyżak, CEO and founder at Ornaq, reflecting on the research .
An Anthropic spokesperson told DCD that the company was working to add new power generation to serve its data centers so that it isn't drawing on supply used by local homes and businesses.
"Much of that new power is natural gas, which can be brought online quickly, ramps up and down as demand changes, and is abundant in the places we’re considering for data centers," the spokesperson said. "We’re also working to broaden our energy mix with geothermal, wind, solar, and emerging technologies, and in regions with strong renewable resources, we’re designing projects that will rely on renewable energy."
The AI firm also pointed to several sustainability measures it has undertaken to address emissions, including joining the carbon emission buying consortium Frontier, and working with Watershed, a carbon accounting and emissions disclosure platform.
The news comes as the company completes its initial public offering this week, which is expected to see the company valued at approximately $1.5 trillion, after shares were priced at $83 ahead of its debut on the Nasdaq.
Major data center firms have increasingly turned to on-site natural gas to bypass the multi-year interconnection queues for a firm grid connection. Microsoft , Meta , Amazon , and Google have all signed deals in recent years for large-scale gas generators to power data centers in the US market.

# Meta to reevaluate net-zero timeline on the back of record emissions

Company reported a 45 percent increase in carbon footprint due to AI demand

November 20, 2026

By

Zachary Skidmore

Have your say

Social networking firm Meta is reevaluating its 2030 net-zero timeline amid record carbon emission levels, according to its latest sustainability report .
In the report, the company revealed its net carbon footprint increased by 45 percent in the last year, hitting 11.9 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent (mtCO2e). The company’s location-based emissions inventory was recorded at almost twice that amount, at 21.7 million mtCO2e.

– Getty Images

Rachel Peterson, Meta’s VP of data centers, and Blair Swedeen, its global head of net zero and sustainability, wrote that the company is “re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones.” That includes the 2030 net zero timeframe and its near-term intensity targets. They said demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than expected, while interconnection queues, permitting, and transmission buildout have lagged. Meta did not give a new date and said it will share the outcome later.
"The path forward is complex, and the route may continue to evolve, but the outcomes we are working toward remain unchanged: to establish a long-term pathway to net zero emissions, to restore more water than we consume, and to build infrastructure in a way that supports surrounding communities and grids," they said in a statement.
The numbers reflect growing emissions across all the major hyperscalers, with Amazon, Google, and Microsoft all reporting double-digit increases in their latest sustainability reports.
Google saw an 18 percent year-on-year increase, with Amazon reporting a 16 percent increase and Microsoft revealing that its emissions had grown by 25 percent. Of the hyperscalers, Meta is the only company to announce a reevaluation of its 2030 commitment, acknowledging the rise, which it attributes to the expansion of AI data centers.
Much of the emissions growth is tied to increasing reliance on natural gas to circumvent grid connection delays in the US. The report stated that Meta may deploy on-site gas where utilities cannot deliver power and plans to buy low-methane certificates to offset some of its emissions. The company left the RE100 climate initiative in July this year, saying it could no longer meet the technical criteria because of investments in new gas power. Last year, the company signed a deal with utility Entergy to fund the construction of ten natural gas plants to power its up to 5GW Hyperion data center in Richland Parish, Louisiana.
The company reported that its electricity consumption rose 35 percent to 24.8TWh, but claimed it matched all of it with clean and renewable energy, stating that it has contracted more than 30GW of low-carbon power, almost 12GW of which is operational. results:
The BIS interim final rule "Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors" was released on November 16, 2026 and took effect on November 19, 2026, the day it was published in the Federal Register. Sources differ on the release date: one law firm alert says November 15 ([WilmerHale](https://www.wilmerhale.com/en/insights/client-alerts/20261117-us-government-restricts-remote-access-to-advanced-ai-chips-and-formally-rescinds-the-ai-diffusion-rule)), while the Pillsbury and K&L Gates alerts and the BIS-linked coverage say November 16 ([Pillsbury](https://www.pillsburylaw.com/en/news-and-insights/commerce-restricts-remote-access-advanced-chips.html), [K&L Gates](https://www.klgates.com/thought-leadership/BIS-Targets-Remote-Access-to-Advanced-Computing-New-Controls-for-Semiconductor-Companies-and-Data-Centers-11-18-2026)).

Key points from the results:

- **Scope:** The rule covers exports, reexports, and in-country transfers to data centers worldwide that give end users access to large amounts of computing power, and it is not limited to future shipments ([Morgan Lewis](https://www.morganlewis.com/pubs/2026/11/commerce-targets-remote-access-to-advanced-semiconductors-in-new-interim-final-rule)).
- **Country-specific licensing:** A separate license requirement now applies to advanced chip exports to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand ([Greenberg Traurig](https://www.gtlaw.com/de/insights/2026/11/bis-interim-final-rule-targets-remote-access-to-advanced-semiconductors-rescinds-ai-diffusion-rule)).
- **AI Diffusion Rule:** The rule formally rescinds the prior AI Diffusion Rule while keeping other advanced computing controls in place ([Morgan Lewis](https://www.morganlewis.com/pubs/2026/11/commerce-targets-remote-access-to-advanced-semiconductors-in-new-interim-final-rule)).
- **Chinese firms:** Reporting focuses on closing an overseas data center route that Chinese firms could use to reach US chips hosted abroad, including in Southeast Asia ([SCMP](https://www.scmp.com/tech/article/3374639/us-tightens-ai-chip-export-curbs-close-chinas-overseas-data-centre-loophole)).
- **Comment period:** Comments are due 60 days after publication, but the rule applies during that period ([Morgan Lewis](https://www.morganlewis.com/pubs/2026/11/commerce-targets-remote-access-to-advanced-semiconductors-in-new-interim-final-rule)).
- **Compliance:** Exporters and foreign data centers are expected to vet their customers, including direct or indirect ownership or control ties ([Beyond TMRW](https://beyondtmrw.org/article/us-sets-licence-rule-for-chinese-access-to-ai-chips-in-overseas-data-centres)).

The official BIS press release describes the rule as designed to stop existing restrictions from being circumvented through remote computing in third countries ([BIS](https://bis.gov/press-release/bis-issues-rule-addressing-remote-access-american-super-intelligence-technology)). The search did not return the Federal Register text itself, so the specific regulatory provisions should be checked against the published rule.

[2611.25325] Pandora's Toolbox Or Why Agent Safety Cannot Be Verified

Skip to main content

# Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence

arXiv:2611.25325 (cs)

[Submitted on 19 Nov 2026]

# Title: Pandora's Toolbox Or Why Agent Safety Cannot Be Verified

Authors: Mario Franco , Carlos Gershenson
View a PDF of the paper titled Pandora's Toolbox Or Why Agent Safety Cannot Be Verified, by Mario Franco and Carlos Gershenson

View PDF
HTML (experimental)

Abstract: Present artificial intelligence agents are constructed by means of a coupling between a fixed language model with a general computing device. We show that this coupling makes safety undecidable. In particular, we show that given some dangerous program, no algorithm can predict whether an agent will run such a program that is semantically equivalent. In general, guardrails, blacklists, whitelists and certifications can only lead to imperfect safety solutions. Under finite constraints (bounded context, values and running time) safety is decidable but still intractable. Specifically, the problem is $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-complete even when the description of the agent is known. Finally, safety is not a compositional property, i.e., agents that can be proven safe on their own can still produce unsafe behavior when grouped together. We also discuss relaxed notions of safety that could be used in practice.

Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

# Title: Why Do LLMs Help with Scientific Misconduct Requests and What to Do About It?: Increasing the Trustworthiness of AI for Science

Authors: Almene De Meran Meguimtsop , Daniel E. Acuna
View a PDF of the paper titled Why Do LLMs Help with Scientific Misconduct Requests and What to Do About It?: Increasing the Trustworthiness of AI for Science, by Almene De Meran Meguimtsop and Daniel E. Acuna

View PDF
HTML (experimental)

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) support scientific research, but some of that assistance can also undermine research integrity. Existing safety evaluations in science often measure whether models refuse misconduct requests, but rarely explain whether they even recognize the problem or why they comply. We investigate this gap across 8 LLMs using SciIntBench, an existing benchmark of 1,350 prompts about scientific research integrity. We examine the reasons behind compliance in four steps. First, when asked directly whether fulfilling a request would involve misconduct, models overwhelmingly identify such requests, even in the Most Covert cases (91%), while they refuse to carry out the request in only 34% of cases. Second, we examine which request characteristics are associated with refusal using features that capture how the request is framed, how much the assistant has been told about what it is helping to hide, and how the goal and the user's stake are stated, among others. Third, we estimate that the most significant effect was to rephrase requests as questions about permissibility rather than instructions, which increased refusal from 52% to 88%. Finally, we test two system-prompt fixes: asking models to assess the request before responding and reminding them of responsible conduct of research principles. These changes increase refusal rates on adversarial requests from 58% to 87% and 86%, respectively. Our findings show that models recognize wrongful requests but still help users violate integrity. Understanding why these failures occur and testing ways to reduce them offer promising paths toward more trustworthy AI for science.

# Title: Physics of Language Models: Part 4.2, Canon Layers at Scale where Synthetic Pretraining Resonates in Reality

Authors: Zeyuan Allen-Zhu
View a PDF of the paper titled Physics of Language Models: Part 4.2, Canon Layers at Scale where Synthetic Pretraining Resonates in Reality, by Zeyuan Allen-Zhu

View PDF
HTML (experimental)

Abstract: Do standard benchmarks see the architectural differences that matter? We study it with 64 from-scratch pretraining runs of Transformers and three linear-model families at 1.3-8B parameters on 1-2T Nemotron-CC tokens, at a cost of roughly 100k USD per 8B run.

In academic-scale pretraining (1.3B parameters, 100B tokens), architectural differences can all but disappear when the models are carefully tuned. Instead, at 1-2T tokens they become measurable: Canon layers, which add local token mixing, consistently improve Transformers, saving about 30% of pretraining tokens for the same MMLU accuracy at 8B. We also introduce GLA5 and GDN2, which improve gated linear attention and Gated DeltaNet with low-rank output gates. Surprisingly, with Canon, the simplest linear model, gated linear attention, matches Gated DeltaNet and outperforms Mamba2 even at 8B/1T. Therefore, the extra machinery of Gated DeltaNet and Mamba2 may do little more than mix neighboring tokens.

Even at 8B/1T, however, high scores on standard benchmarks can hide weaknesses in basic in-context skills. In particular, linear models that match or beat Transformers on these benchmarks cannot, in fact, reliably retrieve information from a short 500-token context. Moreover, no model, Transformer or linear, reliably beats random guessing on arguably the simplest two-hop question, stated in a few short sentences, even at this scale.

These findings $\textbf{challenge traditional architecture research}$ based primarily on standard benchmark scores. In contrast, small synthetic playgrounds, which predicted the architectural differences above at <100M parameters, can reveal what these benchmarks miss. For practitioners, one lesson is to include in-context reasoning examples in pretraining data from an early stage, rather than reserve them for later mid-training, let alone post-training.
