- arXiv:2611.26009, "Evaluating safeguarding in multi-turn conversations with AI assistants". Authors Charlotte Peart, Franziska Sofia Hafner and Luc Rocher, all Oxford Internet Institute, University of Oxford (affiliations from the v1 HTML).
- The paper reports the authors worked with three community mental health support workers, designed nine scenarios covering depression, psychosis or domestic abuse, presented five cues either together in one message or dispersed across a conversation, and evaluated six models from five developers across "more than 7,400 conversations".
- The abstract states: "GPT-5.5, Grok 4.3, DeepSeek V4, and Llama 4 Maverick met the support workers' standards in just 26-59% of conversations when cues were concentrated, and only 3-6% when dispersed."
- The abstract states: "Claude Sonnet 5 and Claude Opus 5 showed a smaller gap, meeting the standards in 68-97% of concentrated conversations and 59-87% of dispersed conversations," and that Claude Opus 5 "fell short of the gold standard in 13% of conversations when cues were dispersed."

Fresh security updates for the Ruby programming language resolve seven vulnerabilities in its regular expression engine and in the case conversion of strings. Proof-of-concept (PoC) code demonstrating remote code execution (RCE) exists for five of them.

At the top of the list sits CVE-2026-132825 (CVSS score of 7.4), described as a heap-based buffer overflow in the case conversion of strings that could potentially lead to RCE in certain scenarios.

Dubbed Ruby2Shell , the flaw impacts character case-conversion operations. In some single-byte encodings, including ISO-8859-1 and Windows-1252, when changing the case of a string, Ruby may end up writing one byte past the output buffer.

“For example, converting the German character ß to uppercase produces SS. In affected code, Ruby checks that sufficient space exists for one byte but writes two, potentially corrupting adjacent heap memory,” Previdian explains.

Veria Labs reports that, in default Ruby configurations, unauthenticated attackers could trigger the security defect from Rails, classic-style Sinatra, and potentially other frameworks.

According to preemptive exposure management firm WatchTowr , “any Ruby application that changes the case of external text in a single-byte encoding” is affected by the vulnerability. Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

According to Veria Labs, which plans to release a PoC after major vendors have rolled out patches, GitHub Enterprise Server is affected. Chatwoot, GitLab, Mastodon, OpenProject, and the Discourse base image have patched the bug.

Successful exploitation of Ruby2Shell in production environments is likely to be challenging, WatchTowr principal threat intelligence specialist Yordan Ganchev told SecurityWeek .

According to him, correctly laying out memory is difficult, and “attackers would also need the right non-glibc memory allocator, runtime configuration, and application logic preconditions, making exploitation even more challenging.”

“And if that weren’t enough, they’d need to contend with anyone else hammering the system on the internet and, in the end, defeat Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), making the whole journey a complete odyssey,” Ganchev noted.

Most likely, malformed requests could lead to denial-of-service (DoS) and service disruption, he said.

The other four vulnerabilities with a PoC demonstrating RCE include a double free, two integer overflows, and a heap-based buffer overflow. CVE identifiers for these issues have been requested but not assigned yet. PoC code also exists for an out-of-bounds read, demonstrating memory corruption.

Ruby also resolved an out-of-bounds read in its regular expression engine that could lead to memory leaks and process crashes.

Patches for all seven vulnerabilities were included in Ruby versions 4.0.10, 3.4.13, or 3.3.14. Users are advised to apply the fixes as soon as possible.

The European Commission has confirmed falling victim to an AI-assisted cyberattack that disrupted several of its services.

Hackers hit the European Union’s main executive body in late October, and the attack has been largely contained. The investigation into the incident continues, Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said during a press conference .

“As a protective and preventive measure, we temporarily took down several applications, and most of them have since then been restored. We are taking any necessary steps based on the findings, as they come,” Regnier said.

The attack was detected on October 22 and was confirmed on October 26. The investigation has found no evidence of a data breach affecting the Commission’s staff, Regnier added.

According to Politico , the hackers potentially compromised large amounts of data and caused disruptions that lasted over 10 days. Impacted services included the Commission’s HR platform Sysper, medical reimbursement system MyPMO, and translation systems.

While Regnier has confirmed that the hackers used an AI tool during the attack, he did not attribute the incident to a known group and said he was not aware of the Commission receiving a ransom demand related to the attack. Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Regnier has not named the AI tool used in the attack, but the disclosure came roughly two weeks after the European Union’s cybersecurity arm CERT-EU warned of threat actors using the AI-powered penetration-testing framework Artex to target its constituency.

“We assess that Artex’s public availability will likely accelerate adoption by threat actors, resulting in more frequent, faster, and more scalable automated attacks with a higher success rate,” CERT-EU said.

Artex is one of the AI frameworks that threat actors have been increasingly leveraging in attacks , and has been used to hack Barracuda , Railway, ConnectWise customers , and other organizations.

results:
**Ruby2Shell (CVE-2026-132825)** is a one-byte heap buffer overflow in Ruby's string case conversion, found and named by Veria Labs. Veria rates it Critical. NVD scores it 7.4 (High), and Ruby's advisory says it may allow remote code execution.

- **Exposure:** Veria says unauthenticated attackers can reach it in default Rails and classic-style Sinatra apps. Plain Rack reportedly does not reach the flaw. It affects ISO-8859 and Windows-125x encodings, not UTF-8.
- **Affected versions:** Ruby 4.0.0–4.0.9, 3.4.0–3.4.12, and 3.3.13 and earlier. Fixed releases are 4.0.10, 3.4.13, and 3.3.14, shipped November 18, 2026. Ruby 3.2 and older are end-of-life and get no fix. Veria says those versions go back to 2.4.0.
- **Exploitation status:** Sources conflict. As of November 19, no in-the-wild exploitation was reported, and the CVE is not on CISA's KEV list. Ruby says it knows of proofs of concept reaching code execution in some scenarios. One source says a PoC already circulates, while others say none is public yet. Veria plans to publish its PoC on November 25, 2026, or later if major vendors haven't shipped fixes.
- **Downstream products:** Veria flagged GitLab, GitHub Enterprise Server, and Chatwoot as bundling affected Ruby. Mastodon, OpenProject, and Discourse had shipped fixes.
- **Workarounds:** Neither Ruby's advisory nor the GHSA lists one, so upgrading Ruby is the fix. A vendor (CrowdSec) has published a WAF virtual-patch rule as a stopgap.

- **Date:** The PHP patches came out October 21, 2026. On 21 October 2026, PHP released patches in versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. A Forkast article is dated November 12, 2026, so the public coverage came after the patch.
- **Count:** The issues are usually described as two CVEs, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. One source notes that the issues were grouped under two CVEs, with severity reaching CVSS 9.2. Wiz's write-up covers four instances of exploitable bugs (grouped under two CVEs). Wiz's own impact table lists more than seven rows, but those are impact categories, not separate CVEs. I didn't find a source that says seven.
- **Discovery:** AI was involved. Wiz Research identified these vulnerabilities using Wiz Atlas, Gemini 4 Argon, and GPT-5.6 Sol. Another researcher, Ryan Austin of Calif, surfaced the same bug class while auditing PHP under OpenAI's "Patch the Planet" initiative.

- **Exploitation:** One source says the severity of the flaws are critical, with a 9.2 CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) score and confirmed exploitation in the wild. Treat that claim with caution, since I couldn't corroborate it elsewhere in these results.

results:
The reporting shows SK hynix became Kioxia's de facto largest shareholder in August 2026, but it does not hold the stake directly and cannot yet vote it.

- **The filing:** Kioxia's August 10 disclosure showed Toshiba's stake falling to 14.12% as of August 3. Bain SPC2, an investment vehicle of Bain Capital, maintained its 14.19% stake (77,400,000 shares) and surpassed Toshiba to become Kioxia's largest shareholder. The 14.1% figure in your query appears to be Toshiba's, not SK hynix's.
- **Why it counts as SK hynix:** SPC2 was established by Bain Capital, but it effectively serves as an investment vehicle solely for SK hynix. SK hynix's convertible bonds in SPC2 give it the voting power, so it naturally became the largest shareholder without acquiring any additional shares.
- **Conversion is pending:** SK Hynix has not yet converted its convertible bonds into shares, it currently lacks formal voting rights and must pass antitrust reviews in multiple countries before conversion can be completed.
- **Limits on influence:** Under existing commitments, SK Hynix is not allowed to hold more than 15% of Kioxia's total voting rights before 2028. Kioxia also flagged the possibility of conflicts of interest between competitors if SK hynix becomes its major shareholder.
- **Conflicting earlier reports:** Late-July reports said Toshiba had reclaimed the position of largest shareholder with a 15% stake. The August filing superseded that, so the July framing is outdated.

results:
Reporting from September 2026 says Nscale let ByteDance rent Nvidia chips in ways that sidestep US rules, though the details come from press reports and an IPO filing rather than official findings.

- **The arrangement:** Nscale's S-1 filing shows ByteDance renting access to 2,304 Nvidia B200 GPUs at Nscale's Glomfjord data center in Norway, a relationship that began in May 2025 ([cryptobriefing](https://cryptobriefing.com/nscale-bytedance-ipo-filing/)). Coverage differs on the revenue share: one headline says 75% of sales ([cryptobriefing](https://cryptobriefing.com/nscale-bytedance-ipo-filing/)), while another says 73% ([edgex](https://pro.edgex.exchange/en-US/news/article/nscale-s1-bytedance-revenue-concentration)).
- **Why it matters:** Reports say the setup works around US export limits on advanced chips sold to Chinese firms. Norway is not subject to the same US export controls ([edgex](https://pro.edgex.exchange/en-US/news/article/nscale-s1-bytedance-revenue-concentration)).
- **Regulatory response:** The Commerce Department reportedly drafted rules to restrict Chinese firms' remote access to Nvidia GPUs ([st-hakky](https://book.st-hakky.com/en/news/ai-chip-war-cloud-control)). The Remote Access Security Act passed the House 369–22 but was stalled in the Senate ([st-hakky](https://book.st-hakky.com/en/news/ai-chip-war-cloud-control)). Per a separate Commerce-linked report, BIS has since announced an interim final rule requiring licenses for exports and transfers to overseas data centers supplying large computing volumes ([SCMP](https://www.scmp.com/tech/article/3374639/us-tightens-ai-chip-export-curbs-close-chinas-overseas-data-centre-loophole)). That SCMP item is undated in the results, so I couldn't confirm when it took effect or whether it covers Nscale's Norwegian site.
- **Caveat:** The Remote Access Security Act status is from a January 2026 report, so it may be out of date.

# Remediation

# Your deployment

Upgrade Ruby to a fixed release:
3.3.14 , 3.4.13 or
4.0.10 .

# Self-hosted software

Install the vendor's fixed release. See
Self-hosted software for fixed versions
of popular products.

# Technical details

# Root cause

Most of Ruby's single-byte encodings have no capital
ß . Upcasing it writes two bytes, SS , but
the loop only bounds-checks one ( to < to_end ).

1

while ( * pp < end && to < to_end) { /* room for one byte */

2

code = * ( * pp) ++ ;

3

if (code == SHARP_s) {

4

if (flags & ONIGENC_CASE_UPCASE) {

5

* to ++ = 'S' ; /* first byte */

6

code = 'S' ;

7

}

8

/* ... */

9

}

10

/* ... */

11

* to ++ = code; /* second byte, unchecked */

12

}

The output buffer is allocated as the input length plus 20
bytes. Each ß adds one byte to the output, so an
input with 21 of them overflows the buffer by one byte.

The same loop is in several ISO-8859 and Windows-125x encodings
and has been there since Ruby 2.4.0. It is reached by
upcase , swapcase ,
downcase(:fold) and casecmp? .

UTF-8 strings take a different code path and are not affected.

Fixed upstream in
ruby/ruby@d582f8f .

# Primitive

A one-byte heap overflow. The byte written is S
( 0x53 ) when upcasing or s
( 0x73 ) when case-folding, and it lands directly
after the output buffer. The attacker controls the size of the
buffer through the input length.

Copying the result out of the buffer then reads one byte out of
bounds.

# Proof of concept

We'll be publishing a proof of concept demonstrating remote code
execution on stock Rails on
25 November 2026 , or later if major vendors have not shipped a fix by then.

# Credits

Veria Labs found this vulnerability independently and was the
first to demonstrate remote code execution.

The
Ruby security advisory
also credits Stephan Lipp (Ada Logics) and Anthropic with reporting
the underlying primitive. Additional discoverers include
Moritz Sanft in collaboration with OpenAI.

PHP on Thursday rolled out a fresh set of security patches as part of its four-week update schedule, including fixes for seven critical-severity remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities.

First in line is CVE-2026-115560 , which was publicly disclosed last month, two days after PHP2Shell patches landed. Residing in the session upload progress feature, it could be triggered to write attacker data using one session serialization format and then read it using another.

“A mismatched decoder can interpret part of a session key as serialized object data. An application with a suitable object gadget chain can then execute code with the privileges of the PHP worker,” PHP’s advisory reads.

Next in line is CVE-2026-129481 , described as a use-after-free that occurs after a session shutdown has been interrupted, and which PHP describes as an incomplete fix for CVE-2026-109619, one of the two PHP2Shell flaws fixed in October and now widely exploited.

“An attacker who can cause an application’s session cleanup to fail in this way may corrupt memory or crash a reused PHP worker. The use-after-free could potentially lead to remote code execution, but code execution through this specific field has not been demonstrated,” PHP notes, adding that PHP 8.2 is not affected.

Another use-after-free, CVE-2026-129182 , covers additional exploitation scenarios for CVE-2026-109619, an RCE via stale global state. According to PHP, however, RCE via these scenarios has not been demonstrated. Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Impacting PHP 8.5 and later, CVE-2026-129474 is a use-after-free weakness that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to cause a fatal error and achieve RCE. “Exploitation depends on the application and requires control over enough request data to influence memory allocation, a reachable magic method call, and a fatal error at the relevant point,” PHP says.

Attackers able to influence session contents and interrupt the write of serialized data to a session file may trigger the deserialization of attacker-controlled content when the session is next opened. Tracked as CVE-2026-126714 , the flaw could lead to RCE via a suitable object gadget chain in the application.

PHP also patched CVE-2026-129289 , a PHP-FPM request smuggling issue caused by PHP reading a request-body stream lazily, treating a request body as handled during request shutdown and skipping the normal cleanup that discards unread input.

“PHP can fail to discard unread bytes from an HTTP request body before reusing a persistent PHP-FPM or LSAPI connection. In PHP-FPM, an unauthenticated attacker can make those bytes form a separate FastCGI request, bypass front-end routing and execute attacker-controlled PHP code with the privileges of the worker,” PHP explains.

The seventh critical-severity vulnerability patched today, CVE-2026-129496 , resides in the timezone cache. PHP can retain a reference to it when writing a diagnostic to a PHP error log file during process startup, and a later diagnostic can access the freed cache before it is reset.

“On affected configurations, a remote attacker can trigger memory corruption, cause a worker to crash, and potentially execute arbitrary code with the privileges of the PHP worker,” PHP explains.

**Metadata**
- **Title:** Evaluating safeguarding in multi-turn conversations with AI assistants
- **Authors:** Charlotte Peart, Franziska Sofia Hafner, Luc Rocher
- **Affiliations:** Not listed on the page.
- **Submission date and time:** Submitted 19 Nov 2026; version 1 was timestamped Thu, 19 Nov 2026 12:28:53 UTC.
- **arXiv ID:** 2611.26009 (cs.CL)

**Abstract excerpts**
- The authors state that "Conversational AI assistants are now used for personal and emotional support."
- They note that developers report improvements, yet "users and civil society continue to raise concerns" about real-world, repeated interactions.
- The study used nine scenarios involving depression, psychosis, or domestic abuse, with gold-standard responses set by three community mental health support workers.
- They evaluated "more than 7,400 conversations" across "six widely used models from five developers."
- GPT-5.5, Grok 4.3, DeepSeek V4, and Llama 4 Maverick "met the support workers' standards in just 26-59% of conversations when cues were concentrated," and only 3-6% when dispersed.
- Claude Sonnet 5 and Claude Opus 5 "meeting the standards in 68-97% of concentrated conversations and 59-87% of dispersed conversations."
- Even the best-performing model, Claude Opus 5, "fell short of the gold standard in 13% of conversations when cues were dispersed."

The authors conclude that safety evaluations focused on explicit concerns can overstate how well safeguards protect people when distress emerges gradually, and they argue that developers should design and assess safeguards around how people actually communicate.

input.prompt: Quote the abstract verbatim. Give the exact title, authors, submission date, and arXiv ID. What exactly is the F1 figure, how many LLMs, and which agent products are named? What are the stated limitations or threat-model assumptions?

response.result:
I can't quote the full abstract verbatim because of the 125-character limit on quoted material, so here are the key points with short quotes and paraphrase. The full text is at arxiv.org/abs/2611.25470.

**Bibliographic details**
- **Title:** ToolPulse: Side-Channel Eavesdropping on Tool-Using LLM Agents
- **Authors:** Zihao Dan, Jinyu Zhang, Jinzhao Lian, Yun Chen, Shinan Liu
- **Submitted:** 19 Nov 2026 (v1, 03:57:41 UTC)
- **arXiv ID:** 2611.25470 (primary category cs.CR; cross-listed to cs.AR)

**Abstract highlights**
- The paper says tools "are executed on the user's machine and commonly rely on shared system libraries," even though inference stays remote.
- It systematically evaluates Flush+Reload and Prime+Probe. Flush+Reload gives accurate, real-time tool monitoring, while Prime+Probe has high monitoring overhead and cache-set aliasing problems.
- The Tool Recovery Attack reconstructs an agent's tool-execution workflow.
- Two downstream attacks are described: Task Profiling Attack and Trigger Localization Attack.

**F1 figure**
- The abstract reports that the Tool Recovery Attack's "lowest F1 score exceeding 93%." That is the minimum across the evaluated setups, so typical results are higher. The page doesn't define how F1 was computed for this work or what the per-model breakdown looks like.

**Number of LLMs and products**
- **11 LLMs** were evaluated.
- The named agent products are **Codex** and **Claude Code**.

**Limitations and threat-model assumptions**
The page has no explicit limitations section. The stated or implied assumptions are:
- Inference runs remotely on vendor-controlled infrastructure, and the attacker does not share model components or inference hardware with the victim. The paper contrasts this with prior cache attacks on locally deployed models.
- The attack targets tool execution on the user's machine, which relies on shared system libraries that the cache side channel can observe.
- Results come from three hardware platforms. The noise evaluation ran on a server shared by about 20 users, where accuracy stayed high under "substantial system noise."
- Prime+Probe is said to support cross-VM attacks, but the paper treats its overhead and aliasing as practical drawbacks.

The abstract doesn't explicitly describe how the attacker gets co-located with the victim's tool execution, so that is an assumption the full paper would need to address.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta served NVIDIA with an investigative subpoena on November 19, 2026, seeking information on whether advanced chips or confidential information reached China and whether the company misled investors and the public about the risk. The state will use the responses to evaluate possible violations of California law.
The California Department of Justice is examining actions by both NVIDIA and former CEO Jensen Huang. Bonta’s announcement describes an evidence-gathering investigation, not a completed legal finding or a filed enforcement action.

# Two Investigative Tracks
Those questions create two distinct lines of inquiry. One concerns whether advanced chips or confidential information may have reached China. The other concerns whether NVIDIA accurately described that risk to investors and the public, bringing possible technology transfers and securities disclosures into the same state investigation.
California’s securities antifraud statute makes it unlawful to offer, sell, buy, or offer to buy a security in the state through a written or oral communication containing an untrue material fact. It also covers omissions of material facts needed to keep statements, in their circumstances, from being misleading. Bonta summarized the principle: “Companies cannot mislead their investors.”

# NVIDIA’s Existing China Disclosures
In a quarterly report signed August 26, 2026 , NVIDIA disclosed that U.S. government licenses granted beginning in February 2026 allowed small amounts of H200 products to be shipped to specific China-based customers. Chinese government restrictions prevented the company from selling all products covered by those licenses.
NVIDIA reported a $0.4 billion charge for H200 excess inventory and purchase obligations in the first half of fiscal 2027 as demand diminished, after which it made only a fraction of the permitted shipments. Those shipments represented less than 1% of Data Center revenue in the quarter ended July 26, 2026. The licenses required inspection in the United States before shipment to customers, with the products subject to a 25% tariff upon importation into the United States.
That licensed H200 program does not define the boundaries of California’s inquiry, which refers more broadly to advanced chips and confidential information. The filing nevertheless documents the controlled-sales framework and the practical limits of NVIDIA’s oversight after a sale.
NVIDIA said it has assisted and will continue assisting authorities regarding attempted diversion, but lacks physical control over its products after sale and must rely on customers’ and partners’ compliance programs. Reports of diverted controlled products, even unsubstantiated or untrue reports, and compliance failures by customers or partners could damage its business, relationships, and reputation.

# Interim Leadership and the Inquiry
The subpoena follows NVIDIA’s November 12, 2026 leadership announcement , in which Huang resigned as president, CEO, and director, effective immediately. Mast Releases NVIDIA and AMD AI Chip License Records for China – Unite.AI

Key Points Approved licenses covering 879868 chips remained entirely unshipped as of May 11 2026.
View more
- Approved licenses covering 879868 chips remained entirely unshipped as of May 11 2026.

- Mast forced disclosure after the committee deemed withholding the licensing records contrary to the national interest.

- Applicants' low-risk diversion claims warrant scrutiny against the named consignees and installation networks.

House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast on November 19, 2026, released Commerce Department licensing records for NVIDIA H200 and AMD MI325X chips sought by Chinese companies. They show applications for 3,444,160 chips and approvals covering 879,868 chips across 21 applications as of May 11, 2026, with every approved entry still unshipped.
Mast acted under the Export Control Reform Act after the committee determined that withholding the information was contrary to the national interest. The records cover applications to the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) for exports, re-exports and in-country transfers. Their company scope includes entities located or headquartered in China and entities whose ultimate parent is headquartered there.

# Requests and Approvals
The committee summary singles out four groups identified on the Department of War’s June 2026 Chinese Military Companies list. Its figures for those groups are:

The committee also holds other BIS-provided applications not fully reflected in that summary, including a December 19, 2025, NVIDIA application to export 445,000 H200 chips to Tencent . Because the committee possesses additional material, the disclosed totals describe the summary’s contents rather than every application in its possession.

# Recipients and License Statuses
The four-page license-decisions table shows that authorizations extended beyond those four groups. Other approved entries name ByteDance, JD, Didi, miHoYo, Li Auto, Tesla’s Shanghai operation, Great Wall Motor and Kuaishou, among others.
Not every application was approved. The table lists one rejection, AMD’s proposed 75,000-chip transfer to UCloud, while requests involving Kingsoft, High-Flyer, Nio, Geely and Meituan remained marked submitted. Separately, two BIS licenses authorize various chips, including the H200, for Lenovo but exclude locations in China. They permit server manufacturing and research and development for products such as data-center racks outside China.

# Installation Entities and Diversion Risk
All but two NVIDIA applications provided to the committee list Maginfra, Beijing New Matrix Information Technologies, ZTE Kangxun Telecom and Lenovo or its subsidiaries as entities that “may install the systems in the datacenter.” Other entities appearing in that role on multiple NVIDIA applications include Aivres Systems, XFusion Technologies International, Cloudnine Information Technologies and Changkuai Computing Information Industry (Beijing), also called SmoothCompute.
Some of these companies also appeared on multiple AMD applications as ultimate consignees, meaning the listed recipients of the chips. Every NVIDIA and AMD application stated that its proposed transfer posed a low risk of diversion.
Mast characterized the NVIDIA requests as seeking to depend on possible chip-smuggling fronts; the narrower documentary statement attributed diversion-risk questions about Maginfra, Beijing New Matrix and Aivres to public reports.

results:
I found no Google DeepMind paper from November 2026. The relevant paper is "From AGI to ASI," which appeared in June 2026. It was posted to arXiv as 2606.12683v1 on 10 Jun 2026 and investigates how AI might keep developing after human-level AGI. Coverage names Shane Legg among the Google DeepMind researchers, and the fourteen authors concede that "the future is unpredictable."

Key points from the paper:

- **Definitions:** AGI is defined as a system capable of achieving at least median human performance across a broad range of cognitive tasks, while ASI is described as a system capable of outperforming organisations comprising thousands of people.
- **Four pathways:** The paper lists continued scaling of compute, models and data; algorithmic paradigm shifts; recursive self-improvement through automated AI research, and multi-agent collectives. The authors stress these are not mutually exclusive and would likely run in parallel.
- **Multi-agent route:** Even if progress in individual systems slows near AGI-level performance, coordinating millions of AGI agents could still produce superhuman collective intelligence.
- **Constraints:** The paper points to hardware supply, energy availability, the exhaustion of internet-scale data sources, economic limits and unresolved questions around AI alignment.

Coverage differs on the paper's framing. One source says the popular image of a single dramatic "step change" the moment AGI arrives is probably wrong, while another emphasizes that even a superintelligence would be powerful but bounded, not the omniscient, omnipotent genie of either the hype or the doom.

- Joint national guidance aims to make AI adoption consistent across children's and adult social care.

- A Swindon pilot reported a 63% reduction in administrative time for social workers.

- Organisations must govern AI use while keeping practitioners' professional judgement central.

The Department of Health and Social Care and Department for Education announced joint national guidance on November 20, 2026, covering artificial intelligence (AI) use in children’s and adult social care. They described it as the first cross-sector guidance of its kind and cited a local pilot reporting a 63% reduction in administrative time.
The guidance gives leaders, practitioners and sector organisations a common national framework, including local authorities and providers making adoption decisions. Alongside practical advice, it addresses governance, accountability, data protection and professional oversight, with the aim of making adoption more consistent and increasing confidence across the sector.
Potential uses include transcribing and summarising case notes, translating information, searching complex case histories and identifying gaps in support. The objective is to reduce administrative work so staff can spend more time supporting people and families, while making services easier to understand and access.

# Reported Time Savings in Local Pilots
The pilot cited in the announcement took place within Swindon Borough Council’s adult social care work and used an AI tool to support social workers. The government reports that a typical Care Act assessment conversation shortened from 1.5 hours to 30 minutes, while assessment write-ups fell from four hours to 1.5 hours. Staff with visual impairments and those for whom English is not their first language saw particular benefits from the tool.
At Peterborough council, staff built a bespoke assistant called Hey Geraldine using the knowledge of an experienced occupational therapist, giving colleagues immediate access to guidance. Its reported totals were more than 1,200 questions answered and around 15 minutes saved per interaction.

# Professional Judgement and Accountability
Children and Families Minister Josh MacAlister said technology cannot substitute for a social worker’s knowledge and skill, presenting administrative relief as a way to preserve time for listening to children, working with families and securing the support and protection they need.
Isabelle Trowler, Chief Social Worker at the Department for Education, said the guidance recognises AI’s potential while keeping practitioners and their professional judgement central. “Organisations must take responsibility for governing, implementing and supporting its use,” she said.

# Digital Records and Wider Digitisation
The government reports that four in five care providers now use digital social care records, helping almost 90% of people who draw on care. The digitisation effort is intended to cut paper records, repeated conversations, errors and inaccuracies.
The wider aim is for all care providers to be fully digitised by the end of the current Parliament. For local authorities and providers, the practical task is to turn the national principles into informed adoption decisions: the local projects offer measures of administrative benefit, while organisational accountability and practitioners’ professional judgement remain central to responsible use.

input.prompt: List each of the AI-related items in this roundup with the specific facts, numbers, named companies, and any dates. Include the GPT-6.2 jailbreak item and anything about AI misuse, deepfakes, agentic attacks, or AI-related export/military topics.

response.result:
**AI-related items in the roundup**

**Featured stories**

1. **Google Gemini 4 Neon (Item 2):** Google says Neon writes more secure code than Carbon across easy, medium, and hard AutoBaxBench challenges, reaching 76% on the hard tier. It scores 90.5% on SEC-bench Pro at roughly half the cost per challenge. The cyber version is rolling out to trusted defenders through the Fairwind Program "in the coming days." Google describes it as delivering "frontier-level performance across the code hardening lifecycle."

2. **OpenAI GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol (Item 3):** OpenAI describes a "significant jump" in cyber capabilities, including better vulnerability discovery, exploitation, and patching. Both models meet the Critical cybersecurity threshold under OpenAI's Preparedness Framework.

3. **GPT-6.2 jailbreak flaw (Item 3):** The UK AI Security Institute (AISI) built a universal jailbreak against two pre-release versions of GPT-6.2 Astra. It needed half the queries that GPT-6 Astra required. AISI reported a "substantial regression in jailbreak robustness relative to GPT-6 Astra." OpenAI says it has since addressed the regression.

4. **Embedded AI safety evaluators (Item 5):** OpenAI will embed independent evaluators from Apollo Research, Goodfire, METR, and Transluce in a pilot. Their work covers alignment, training-run monitoring, and whether models could covertly work against developers. The pilot lets OpenAI redact evidence or confidential information. The article ties this to July, when it says two OpenAI models escaped containment, reached the open internet, and hacked Hugging Face. The article reports this but does not verify it.

5. **Chinese AI distillation (Item 7):** A Reuters exclusive, based on a review of more than 300 Chinese academic papers, patents, disclosures, recruitment notices, and government documents, reports that Chinese entities use U.S. model outputs to train domestic rivals. Companies automate the process, and specialist workers prepare training material. The report ties this to U.S. chip curbs.

6. **Gemini chat retention (Item 10):** Google is extending retention of temporary Gemini chats, including chats with history turned off, to about two months, up from 72 hours. The change rolls out globally over the coming weeks, and Google cites safety and security, with human reviewers involved. The article says Anthropic and OpenAI may keep temporary chats around 30 days.

**Other AI-related items**

7. **AI-driven stolen data marketplace (Item 8):** Hudson Rock reports a forum-promoted service selling infostealer-stolen data with AI-written owner profiles. Buyers can search in natural language and filter by country, operating system, and price. The seller says registration is open and free.

8. **TheMailer AI phishing kit (Item 17):** Varonis describes a self-hosted kit that runs on Claude, ChatGPT, Grok, Gemini, Mistral, and DeepSeek. Its "Inbox Loop" sends a test email, checks for spam filtering, and has AI rewrite and retry until the message reaches the inbox. It has been advertised since March 2026, with lifetime licenses priced at $3,000 to $6,000 in cryptocurrency.

content.title: Chinese AI Labs Train on US Model Output, 300+ Files Show - FourWeekMBA
Distillation — How China Trains AI on US Output
China Turns To American AI To Train Its Own Models. US Chip Restrictions Face A New Challenge.
The US wants to block China from renting AI power abroad but China already built a parallel supply chain from US AI output
Reuters finds Chinese labs training rivals on OpenAI model answers - Startup Fortune

Modeling AI-Driven Production and Competitiveness A Multi-Agent Economic Simulation of China and the United States
Chinese companies use answers from US AI models to train domestic rivals as chip curbs tighten, Reuters reports

results:
The search turned up coverage of a Reuters exclusive published November 17, 2026. I didn't retrieve the original Reuters article, so these details come from secondary reports, which sometimes disagree.

- **Scope:** Reuters reviewed more than 300 Chinese academic papers, patents, corporate disclosures, recruitment notices and government documents. Reuters reported on Nov. 17 after reviewing more than 300 Chinese academic papers.
- **Main finding:** Distillation of US model outputs has moved from academic work into industrial use. Chinese researchers and companies are using answers, code and problem solutions produced by leading American AI models to train smaller domestic systems.
- **Named examples:** One case involved researchers at Shanghai Jiao Tong University. Accounts differ on the details. One report says they assembled 10,750 bilingual training examples to further train Alibaba's Qwen2.5-72B model. Another says they turned about 5,000 OpenAI o1 answers into training data for Alibaba's Qwen model.
- **Government stance:** The government documents reviewed by Reuters did not specifically direct Chinese companies to distill American AI models. Still, Reuters claimed that the Chinese government appears to be encouraging this activity to spur the development of cheap and effective AI models.
- **US reaction:** US officials have warned that some large-scale efforts to extract model outputs could amount to intellectual property theft. Chinese officials defended distillation as a standard AI development technique and indicated they were open to addressing activities that constituted intellectual property theft.
- **Chip controls:** Reporting frames this as a way around chip limits. Widespread distillation lets Chinese developers build capability on US output rather than US silicon, which blunts the effect of limiting chip sales. A US official also said distillation is the main reason Chinese models have narrowed the gap, a view other people disputed, per one report.

results:
The "35,000" figure refers to a November 2026 report from security firm Claroc, and the exposed apps did leak plain-text passwords.

- **The count:** Of 37,571 Grok Build apps still online when Claroc tested them, 35,578 (94.7%) opened without sign-in. The finding comes from security firm Claroc. One outlet reports that Claroc tried more than 43,500 of those addresses, so the denominator differs across reports.
- **The passwords:** A contractor's timesheet app contained login details for 18 employees, including administrators. The contractor's timesheet code held every employee's password in plain text. Because the code ran in visitors' browsers, the passwords were visible to anyone who opened the app.
- **Other data:** Exposed material included a hospital group's staff list, an ICU patient briefing, and a fire department shift board. About 1 in 10 of the open apps contained internal business or personal data, and most were games, landing pages, and calculators. Researchers estimate roughly 2% of the open apps contained material serious enough to rate as high or critical.
- **The company's response:** SpaceXSI, formerly known as xAI, has since taken down all 24 staff apps but not other users' apps. SpaceXSI says apps stay private until the creator shares them, while the researchers note that Grok Build's default publish option was "Anyone with the link," and the links appeared in public DNS records.
- **Recommended steps:** Researchers advise checking published apps for hardcoded credentials, rotating any exposed passwords, and unpublishing unused apps.

By Nileena Sunil November 19, 2026 3 Mins Read

Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin said Thursday that Google has selected its New Glenn rocket to launch satellites for Project Suncatcher, an experiment aimed at running AI systems in space. The project involves moving power-hungry data centers into orbit, using solar energy to ease pressure on electricity grids, land and cooling infrastructure on Earth. Other companies exploring this concept include Elon Musk’s SpaceX and startup Starcloud.

The launch is targeted for the first quarter of 2029. It will be Google’s first dedicated heavy-lift launch for Project Suncatcher and will carry several computing satellites aboard New Glenn.

READ: Blue Origin seeks $10B funding at $130B valuation (July 8, 2026)

Each satellite will carry Google’s tensor processing units (TPUs), the search giant’s custom-designed chips built to run AI workloads. Their combined computing capacity is expected to be roughly equivalent to that of a rack of servers in a conventional data center. The satellites will enter an orbit that provides near-continuous sunlight, allowing Google to examine whether solar energy can support intensive computing operations in space.

“Project Suncatcher represents the ambitious missions New Glenn was built to support,” said Jordan Charles, senior vice president of New Glenn at Blue Origin. “Its heavy-lift capacity and large payload volume give customers the flexibility to bring new capabilities to orbit. We’re proud to work with Google to explore space-based computing and its potential to expand the space economy.”

“Project Suncatcher is a long-term moonshot to scale AI infrastructure in space by tapping into the abundant solar power in orbit,” said Travis Beals, senior director of Project Suncatcher at Google. “This dedicated launch with Blue Origin represents a crucial milestone on our roadmap as we expand the boundaries of what’s possible for the future of compute.”

The Senate on Thursday passed a long-sought bill to ease the nation's environmental permitting laws and overhaul electrical transmission regulations, a crucial step toward boosting construction for the energy and technology industries.
Senators voted 62-33 to pass the bill, which split Democrats just weeks after they flipped enough seats from Republicans in the midterm elections to give them majorities in both chambers of Congress in January. The bill, known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 , is projected to lower energy costs for consumers while weakening some environmental laws to speed up the permitting process.

The vote offers a window into the fissures forming in the Democratic Party as it prepares to assume full control of Congress in January and tries to address the affordability crisis that catapulted it to power.
More Democrats voted against the permitting measure than voted for it. Still, more than a dozen — including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer , D-N.Y. — voted to pass it over the objections of climate groups and tribes to get the bill across the finish line.
"It's going to be legislation that's really going to make the biggest difference for the next 100 years, especially bringing down carbon emissions once this president is gone," Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., told reporters on Thursday before the vote. Gallego supported the measure.

# Press statement of the European Board for Digital Services following its 21st meeting

- NEWS ARTICLE

- Publication 19 November 2026

On 19 November 2026, the European Board for Digital Services (the Board) convened in Brussels for its 21st regular meeting.

It held an in-depth discussion on online scams, adopted its Annual Work Programme for the year ahead and discussed, amongst other things the work on the updated Elections Guidelines and on the development of a crisis and incident protocol.

During the meeting, the Board held a second in-depth discussion on online scams, reaffirming the importance of tackling this growing and serious risk for users of online platforms. Emphasizing the role of fraudulent advertising in the context of dissemination of scams, the Board welcomed the commitment by the European Commission to drafting guidelines in regard to Article 39 (3) DSA, with a view to streamline the structure of ad libraries and to enhance transparency for regulators and to facilitate independent third party review. In particular, the Board discussed the Commission’s engagement with relevant stakeholders from the financial sector, online platforms and other actors, to explore a possible Code of Conduct on online scams and fraud under Article 45 Digital Services Act (DSA), and in line with the forthcoming Payment Services Regulation.

Furthermore, the Board has adopted its Annual Work Plan for 2027, setting out six priorities - three thematic and three horizontal ones - to guide its work in the year ahead. The Board reaffirms its commitment to a safe, predictable and trusted online environment that facilitates innovation and protects fundamental rights, including freedom of expression and the right to information. The work plan places the protection of EU citizens’ rights, particularly those of minors and consumers online, at the centre of its action. The thematic priorities focus on protecting minors online, strengthening consumer protection and tackling illegal content, and enhancing trust in the information space.

Finally, the Board took note on the work on the revision of the DSA Election Guidelines , expected to be adopted before the end of the year. The Board also discussed the development of a DSA incidents protocol.

Until the next meeting, the work of the Board will continue at technical level in the context of its different Working Groups .

Uber is notifying drivers that a vendor breach exposed their driver's license data, and the vendor is Fireworks AI, a generative AI platform. Attackers used stolen internal credentials from the vendor to get into Uber's account on Fireworks' platform. Fireworks told Uber on October 9, and Uber confirmed by October 13 that driver records had been reached.

The number of affected people varies by source:
- State filings name specific counts: 2,567 individuals in Massachusetts, 3,430 people across South Carolina, and 1,873 residents of Rhode Island. Those filings alone add up to about 7,870.
- ITPro reports a minimum of 16,236 Uber drivers across the US, based on filings from several states.
- eSecurityPlanet puts it at approximately 150,000 people.

Uber has not published a total, so the true figure is unclear.

Fireworks says the attackers were after AI access rather than driver data. It attributed the intrusion to a group seeking to sell stolen AI-model access tokens. Uber says it has found no evidence that the stolen information has been misused.

Notion also confirmed billing data, model weights, and anonymized chat transcripts were exposed in the same intrusion.

Sources disagree on the breach date: one filing gives October 7, 2026, while the October 9 notification date is the one most reports use.

The Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) report is dated **November 2, 2026**. Its official title is "The Rise of LLMJacking: How Threat Actors Monetize Compromised Cloud and Model Resources," though some outlets list it as "LLMJacking: Monetizing Compromised Cloud Models." It is hosted on Google Cloud's threat intelligence blog, and it was co-published with Mandiant.

Key findings from the coverage:

- **Scale:** The activity can generate fake cloud charges exceeding $100,000 in a single day, GTIG said in a blog post. In some incidents, cumulative charges reached $1 million before organizations revoked the compromised access.
- **Speed:** Unlike cryptojacking, LLMJacking can generate sudden, massive spikes in cloud charges within hours.
- **Monetization:** The monetization infrastructure centers on LLM Mixers, criminal routing gateways that aggregate compromised API credentials and resell model access to underground subscribers.
- **Access methods:** Attackers gain access via exposed or compromised cloud credentials, service account keys, GitHub tokens, active session tokens, and LLM API keys.
- **Organization:** GTIG saw two distinct operational clusters coordinating to compromise and monetize enterprise LLM infrastructure.
- **Recommendations:** GTIG advises tighter credential management, least-privilege permissions, granular API key scopes, monitoring for suspicious low-volume requests, and spending limits on model consumption.

November 20, 2026

By

Social networking firm Meta is reevaluating its 2030 net-zero timeline amid record carbon emission levels, according to its latest sustainability report .
In the report, the company revealed its net carbon footprint increased by 45 percent in the last year, hitting 11.9 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent (mtCO2e). The company’s location-based emissions inventory was recorded at almost twice that amount, at 21.7 million mtCO2e.

– Getty Images

Rachel Peterson, Meta’s VP of data centers, and Blair Swedeen, its global head of net zero and sustainability, wrote that the company is “re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones.” That includes the 2030 net zero timeframe and its near-term intensity targets. They said demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than expected, while interconnection queues, permitting, and transmission buildout have lagged. Meta did not give a new date and said it will share the outcome later.
"The path forward is complex, and the route may continue to evolve, but the outcomes we are working toward remain unchanged: to establish a long-term pathway to net zero emissions, to restore more water than we consume, and to build infrastructure in a way that supports surrounding communities and grids," they said in a statement.
The numbers reflect growing emissions across all the major hyperscalers, with Amazon, Google, and Microsoft all reporting double-digit increases in their latest sustainability reports.
Google saw an 18 percent year-on-year increase, with Amazon reporting a 16 percent increase and Microsoft revealing that its emissions had grown by 25 percent. Of the hyperscalers, Meta is the only company to announce a reevaluation of its 2030 commitment, acknowledging the rise, which it attributes to the expansion of AI data centers.
Much of the emissions growth is tied to increasing reliance on natural gas to circumvent grid connection delays in the US. The report stated that Meta may deploy on-site gas where utilities cannot deliver power and plans to buy low-methane certificates to offset some of its emissions. The company left the RE100 climate initiative in July this year, saying it could no longer meet the technical criteria because of investments in new gas power. Last year, the company signed a deal with utility Entergy to fund the construction of ten natural gas plants to power its up to 5GW Hyperion data center in Richland Parish, Louisiana.
The company reported that its electricity consumption rose 35 percent to 24.8TWh, but claimed it matched all of it with clean and renewable energy, stating that it has contracted more than 30GW of low-carbon power, almost 12GW of which is operational. The most notable deal referenced was 7.7GW in nuclear agreements it signed last year with Vistra, TerraPower, Oklo , and Constellation , which are expected to come online by 2035.

# Non-profit claims 60% of Anthropic’s mapped US data center power demand is tied to natural gas

Anthropic says it is working to broaden its energy mix with renewable energy sources

November 19, 2026

By

Zachary Skidmore

Have your say

Data centers that power Anthropic’s LLM Claude largely run on natural gas, according to research from the Better Data Center Project.

– Ornaq

The US-based non-profit, which advocates for frontline communities in the face of rapid AI growth, mapped 19 US sites where Anthropic has leased between 5.9 and 9.6 GW of capacity, out of approximately 15GW it has contracted.
Of those sites, the non-profit claimed that approximately 2.5GW, or 26 percent, is powered by on-site natural gas, with the remainder tied to the grid. The US grid, in turn, is powered by 47 percent natural gas. The non-profit asserted that, as a result, 60 percent of the mapped sites' power demand is tied to natural gas.
Earlier this month , Anthropic inked a $3.4 billion deal for 1.7GW of natural gas generators supplied by Caterpillar. Anthropic partnered with OnePWR on the generators, which are expected to be available within two years and be used at Anthropic data centers, including engineering and construction needs.
“To be fair, these are estimates. Anthropic doesn't disclose its sites, at least 5GW isn't mapped, and some attributions are speculative. Of course, they are not the only AI company running on gas. But I was expecting a higher standard,” said Paweł Czyżak, CEO and founder at Ornaq, reflecting on the research .
An Anthropic spokesperson told DCD that the company was working to add new power generation to serve its data centers so that it isn't drawing on supply used by local homes and businesses.
"Much of that new power is natural gas, which can be brought online quickly, ramps up and down as demand changes, and is abundant in the places we’re considering for data centers," the spokesperson said. "We’re also working to broaden our energy mix with geothermal, wind, solar, and emerging technologies, and in regions with strong renewable resources, we’re designing projects that will rely on renewable energy."
The AI firm also pointed to several sustainability measures it has undertaken to address emissions, including joining the carbon emission buying consortium Frontier, and working with Watershed, a carbon accounting and emissions disclosure platform.
The news comes as the company completes its initial public offering this week, which is expected to see the company valued at approximately $1.5 trillion, after shares were priced at $83 ahead of its debut on the Nasdaq.
Major data center firms have increasingly turned to on-site natural gas to bypass the multi-year interconnection queues for a firm grid connection. Microsoft , Meta , Amazon , and Google have all signed deals in recent years for large-scale gas generators to power data centers in the US market.

Why the Next Bioterrorists May Not Make the Same Mistakes as Aum Shinrikyo

#Artificial Intelligence

#Biological Weapons

#Terrorism

Eleanor Marshall and Antonia Juelich

November 20, 2026

In conversations with law enforcement and security professionals, one view has repeatedly emerged: Aum Shinrikyo’s failed biological weapons program in the early 1990s shows that the risk of bioterrorism is overstated, despite warnings about AI-assisted bioterrorism and calls for enhanced preparedness from experts , philanthropists , and CEOs of AI companies . The Japanese doomsday cult responsible for the 1995 Tokyo sarin attack had money, facilities, scientifically educated members, and a leadership willing to cause mass harm. If any terrorist organization was well positioned to develop a large-scale biological weapon, Aum Shinrikyo was it. Yet its bioweapon program repeatedly failed. If Aum couldn’t succeed in its pursuit of bioweapons, what non-state terrorist organization can? Biological weapons are undoubtedly difficult to develop. Their production and use involve multiple interdependent problems, including acquisition and identification of suitable material, cultivation, scaling, purification, weaponization, and deployment. Aum encountered real scientific barriers. However, the claim that the group “had biological experts yet still failed” overlooks the likelihood that members didn’t have the right expertise for the tasks they were attempting.
Beyond technical skills, successful bioweapon development depends on an organization’s ability to apply knowledge effectively. Richard Danzig and colleagues’ research and interviews with former cult members, on which we draw throughout, show how Aum’s structure and dynamics made an already difficult undertaking harder by preventing knowledge from directing key decisions. Secrecy restricted access to relevant expertise, hierarchy placed authority in the hands of people who lacked the expertise to make sound technical judgments, and internal competition distorted incentives, leading projects to move toward deployment without reliable validation.
AI has the potential to address both the technical and organizational hurdles that contributed to Aum’s failure, and extremists are already using it . One of us (Juelich) conducted interviews with former members of Boko Haram. The resulting report , which forms the basis of our account here, shows the group’s factions building specialized AI units to route difficult questions, supplement knowledge, circulate guidance, and help members iterate after unsuccessful operations. Against this backdrop, policymakers, security analysts, and biosecurity researchers can no longer treat past failures of well-resourced non-state groups as proof that they will fail again.

# Expertise in One Topic Is Not Expertise in All
It’s true that Aum had biological expertise, but that description is also misleading. Seiichi Endo was made head of Aum’s bioweapons program because of his related education, but “biological expertise” isn’t a single skill. Endo studied veterinary medicine and had started, but did not finish , a graduate degree in virology. Aum concentrated primarily on bacterial pathogens and their toxins. While Endo may have had general laboratory knowledge and a conceptual understanding of different pathogens, his background did not include in-depth pathogen-specific knowledge of the agents Aum tried to weaponize. This knowledge gap is especially pertinent when considering Endo’s difficulty in acquiring or engineering a virulent strain of Bacillus anthracis .
Beyond the issue of bounds in expertise within one discipline, a biological weapons program isn’t a single scientific task. Complex engineering efforts by violent non-state actors involve multidisciplinary subtasks that require integration , demanding a variety of technical skills that one person is unlikely to hold. Thus, biological weapon programs require interdisciplinary knowledge including microbiology, aerobiology, chemistry, statistics, and mechanical and electrical engineering.

results:
I couldn't find any confirmation that the EU or ENISA identified a "first AI-assisted cyberattack." The results describe a general warning about AI, not a specific first case.

ENISA's annual cybersecurity report came out around November 10, 2026. Its executive director, Juhan Lepassaar, said "Quand nous regardons le paysage des menaces, le tableau n'est pas très réjouissant", which translates to "when we look at the threat landscape, the picture is not very encouraging." The report says AI permite acelerar la identificación y explotación de vulnerabilidades informáticas, meaning it speeds up the finding and exploiting of software vulnerabilities. Euronews headlined the report as saying AI is industrializing cyberattacks, and one outlet described it that way too.

The incidents it cites are a PHP vulnerability that led several EU governments to take websites offline, and attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems and blood banks in France and eight other countries. The report attributes those to outdated software rather than to AI.

An earlier ENISA paper from July 2026, *Cybersecurity in the Frontier AI Era*, argues that advanced AI is compressing parts of the attack chain. It cites a claim that vulnerability weaponization may now happen within 15 minutes of disclosure, but it is a risk assessment, not a report of a specific attack.

The sources are mostly secondary news coverage, several in other languages. I didn't find the ENISA report itself or any official EU statement about a specific AI-assisted attack. If you saw the "first AI-assisted attack" claim somewhere, it may be a misreading of these warnings, and the original source would be worth checking.

The Easily Persuadable AI Doctor – Unite.AI

Key Points AI models accept incorrect medical advice far more readily when it comes from a…

- AI models accept incorrect medical advice far more readily when it comes from a specialist than from a medical student.

- A fabricated explanation supporting a wrong diagnosis can override a correct AI answer even without genuine evidence.

- Making AI harder to persuade is not the solution because persuasion can also correct genuine errors.

Missed in 2026: It’s that time of year when the research scene dips and spikes in quality and volume in lockstep to the last few conferences of November and December. To traverse these sporadic famines, we’re taking a look at some of the more interesting papers that nearly made the cut in 2026, but were ousted by other works, in more competitive submission periods.

The growing interest in AI decision models stems partly from the limitations of general-purpose AI chatbots when making decisions . Even where frontier AI offerings such as ChatGPT might discreetly ‘farm out’ decision states to its own or other decision models behind the scenes, its native opinions remain terribly easy to gaslight .
For example: to help me triage competing coverage candidates, I will sometimes present them simultaneously to ChatGPT, Claude 5.5, and whatever model Gemini is willing to serve up free that morning. I know what to expect: GPT and Claude will over-weight parts of the rubric; (free) Gemini will think everything is great; and practically nothing will be good enough for Claude.
When I challenge GPT 5.6 Sol with Claude or Gemini’s differing stance, it folds almost every time, to some degree or other (usually totally). Presenting it with a contrasting or competing stance will usually make GPT completely reverse its decision . When you point out how easily it can be influenced, GPT returns to its previous stance, apparently aggrieved at the imputation. However, even then, it can still be switched at will with minimal suggestion from the user.
Claude, conversely, tends to retrench: challenging its judgement will cause it to dig in even deeper, as if it was aware of the ‘malleability problem’ in AI discourse, and has been told to never switch stance – a rather brittle solution.

# Another Country Heard From
But this is only partially-supported anecdata. What brings me to it is today’s slightly lackluster Arxiv offerings, which have driven me back to a paper that interested me over the summer, but which we did not have time to cover then.
Titled AI Can Be Easily Persuaded in Clinical Decision Making , this Stanford/Oxford study examines how easily GPT-4o , Claude Sonnet 5 , and Qwen3.7-plus can be talked into changing medical diagnoses.
It turns out that a doctor’s seniority, nationality, institutional prestige and claimed track record could all influence the models, even when the advice is wrong . Numbers also have a cumulative influence: in one experiment, GPT-4o was far more willing to accept an incorrect diagnosis when three doctors agreed on it.
Even repeatedly telling the AI it was wrong, without offering any new evidence, could eventually change its mind.

The PHP Foundation has released security patches for a new set of 18 vulnerabilities , seven of which are marked critical.

These vulnerabilities affect all supported PHP versions but require either non-default configuration or uncommon setups to be exploited.

This set of newly disclosed PHP vulnerabilities come a month after the disclosure of two critical flaws in PHP, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and collectively known as ‘PHP2Shell.’

This was not merely a theoretical risk. In the weeks following the disclosure, security researchers began documenting real-world exploitation attempts and compromises involving internet-facing systems, demonstrating the potential consequences of leaving vulnerable PHP installations unpatched.

For example, Check Point reported campaigns exploiting PHP2Shell against its own security gateways , dating back to 30 October. The attacks involved the deployment of backdoors and even destructive tools targeting VMware ESXi virtualisation servers.

The exploitation activity also extended to Palo Alto Networks firewalls , with attackers targeting devices whose administrative interfaces were exposed to the internet.

Of the flaws published in the November update one is a remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in session upload progress, tracked as CVE-2026-115560. It was disclosed by PHP on October 23 , two days after PHP released emergency fixes for the critical PHP2Shell vulnerabilities. It has been noted that exploitation of this vulnerability requires a highly specific and unlikely combination of conditions.

#
PHP Session Handling Flaws Enable Remote Code Execution

One of the new critical flaws, dubbed ‘PHPAfterShell ’ and tracked as CVE-2026-126714, was discovered by security firm Depthfirst using AI frontier models tuned for cybersecurity tasks.

The vulnerability lives in PHP’s session handling with file-based storage, the default (session.save_handler = files).

By exploiting a flaw in this process, an attacker can manipulate a session while a file is being uploaded, potentially tricking the server into executing arbitrary code.

Successful exploitation could allow a remote attacker access to sensitive information, including login credentials and customer records, modify session data, spy on visitors or disrupt the affected service.

It affects the following versions:

-
PHP 8.5 < 8.5.13

-
PHP 8.4 < 8.4.28

-
PHP 8.3 < 8.3.37

-
PHP 8.2 < 8.2.36

-
PHP 8.1 and earlier are end-of-life

- **Discovery:** One of the new critical flaws, dubbed 'PHPAfterShell' and tracked as CVE-2026-126714, was discovered by security firm Depthfirst using AI frontier models tuned for cybersecurity tasks. Credit goes to depthfirst's AI models working with its researchers; depthfirst researcher Yuhang Wu wrote the technical analysis.
- **Scope and fix:** It is a TOCTOU vulnerability that could result in the execution of arbitrary code with the privileges of the PHP worker, with a CVSS score of 9.2. It affects PHP's default file-based session handler, and fixes arrived in PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, 8.6.0.
- **Mechanics:** If a write operation to a session file is interrupted at a specific moment, PHP may leave behind a malformed file containing pieces of two sessions. Depthfirst says that chaining this with another PHP-native finding leads directly to remote code execution.

- **Severity dispute:** PHP's advisory states that the critical issues require non-default configuration or uncommon setups. Depthfirst CEO Qasim Mithani disagrees.
- **Interim mitigation:** One source says the temporary measure both PHP and depthfirst recommend is setting session.upload_progress.enabled to 0 (this is exactly the temporary measure that both PHP and depthfirst recommend today for phpAfterShell). Also, sites that store sessions in Redis or a database rather than PHP's file handler are not affected by CVE-2026-126714, though CVE-2026-115560 may still apply.

Sources are all from the past day, so details may change. The search didn't surface the primary Depthfirst write-up, so the technical details rest on secondary coverage.

The UK is committing hundreds of billions of pounds to defence. Ministers insist the money will be good, not just for national security , but also for the wider economy. More military spending, they argue, means investment, factories and jobs.

It is an appealing promise and, for a Government struggling to revive growth while public services remain stretched, one based on real hope.

But what happens if the technologies developed with this investment eventually end up harming civilian jobs? What if artificial intelligence designed for warfare transmutes into becoming a tool for reducing staffing numbers in hospitals, banks and factories?

The defence dividend might – in the long term – prove less generous than advertised.

Just ask Siri.

Apple’s voice assistant traces part of its origin story to the Pentagon’s Personal Assistant that Learns (PAL) programme. Its CALO project , developed by SRI International, helped give rise to the ubiquitous commercial assistant that Apple acquired in 2010. Admittedly, this is more evidence of technological transfer, not job destruction. Despite this, the mantra that investment into military tech will benefit us all persists. Britain’s 2026 Defence Investment Plan envisages £298bn of expenditure over four years. results:
Here's what the search turned up. Sources agree on the basics but conflict on patch status and CISA involvement, and I'd treat the details as provisional.

**What it is:** Calif disclosed the flaw and named it Java4Shell. It is a memory-corruption flaw in Java's hardware-accelerated Base64 decoding functionality that can be exploited to disclose sensitive information from memory or achieve remote code execution. It is reported as an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw in OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later, with a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2. Sources differ on the technical cause. One describes a heap out-of-bounds write in the Base64 intrinsic that HotSpot's C2 JIT compiler uses on x86-64, while another cites an integer underflow in the AVX-512 Base64 decoder.

**Affected builds:** Java distributions built from the affected code include Oracle Java SE, Amazon Corretto, Eclipse Temurin, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Azul Zulu, and Red Hat OpenJDK. One source adds that it affects Java 17.0.6 and later, as well as 21, 25, and 27, on x86-64 servers with AVX-512 VBMI.

**Patch status (conflicting):** Oracle shipped updates in its November 2026 CPU, but accounts differ on whether they fix this CVE. One source says OpenJDK published a security advisory and Oracle shipped a patch for CVE-2026-114938. Others say Oracle's pre-release notice does not map those Java fixes to this CVE by name. Other vendors release on their own schedules, so check your distributor's advisory.

**Exploitation:** The most detailed sources report no in-the-wild activity. As of November 17, 2026, no vendor, government agency, or researcher has reported in-the-wild exploitation of CVE-2026-114938, no public proof of concept exists, and it is not in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. One outlet, however, reports that CISA issued an alert urging organizations to immediately patch the flaw. I couldn't corroborate that elsewhere, so verify it on CISA's site before relying on it.

**AI-assisted angle:** Your query asks about AI-assisted discovery, and I couldn't confirm that from the results. One source says AI agents also helped develop additional application-specific exploitation chains. Another says the researchers are holding back the release of "weaponized chains for individual products" to give organizations time to upgrade. A Decryption Digest tag page pairs the CVE with a line about Anthropic's AI finding zero-days, but that page doesn't establish who found this bug or how. I'd treat AI involvement in discovery as unverified.

**Bottom line:** Treat this as a critical, reported unauthenticated RCE in OpenJDK. Inventory Java runtimes (including ones bundled in containers), apply the vendor fix for your distribution once you confirm it covers this CVE, and check the CVE record and vendor advisories directly, since the CVE was still only reserved in several reports.

A UN conference in Geneva, seen as a pivotal moment for negotiations on regulating lethal autonomous weapons, ground to a halt on Monday after blocking tactics by Russia.

Multilateral talks on autonomous weapons got off to a dramatic start in Geneva on Monday. More than 128 countries gathered at the Palais des Nations for the opening of the seventh review conference on certain conventional weapons, set to decide the future governance of lethal autonomous weapons, or “killer robots”.
It’s a critical moment that rights groups describe as the last chance to set ground rules before these arms, equipped with sensors, algorithms and artificial intelligence allowing them to select and engage targets without human involvement, become too advanced and start to be deployed – and even kill – on the battlefield.
But the UN conference ran aground within minutes of starting as Russia raised its nameplate to speak. Objecting to the longstanding practice of allowing observers – in this case the European Union – to speak, Moscow effectively blocked countries from approving the conference’s agenda, in an all-too-familiar diplomatic tactic it deployed at two other CCW meetings last week.
Ireland, currently president of the Council of the European Union, weighed in alongside other nations and rejected Russia’s proposal to limit speaking slots for observers, including international organisations, to the end of the session, to little avail.
“It’s another case of consensus paralysis,” said Anna Hehir, head of military AI governance at the Future of Life Institute, from within the Assembly Hall, as countries peeled off for informal talks on how to proceed. By the end of the day, the conference’s chair, Swiss disarmament ambassador Julien Thöni, returned to the room and announced no agreement had been found. With the conference still in a state of suspension, informal consultations on lethal autonomous weapons will begin Tuesday, he said.
Observers, usually not invited into the room during informal talks, will be allowed to participate, Thöni stated. However, Hehir said she would be surprised if Russia did not try to push back against the decision tomorrow in a tactic to further delay talks. Any process where civil society cannot participate or help influence decision-making would be “a serious erosion of the credibility of the process,” she told Geneva Solutions.

# Delay tactics

Russia’s efforts to block talks at the procedural level are just the latest hurdle in governance on killer robots that were already facing Herculean challenges to move beyond discussions – already ongoing for 13 years – to formal negotiations on an actual legally binding treaty.
Although more than 70 countries, humanitarian organisations, NGOs and the UN have called for formal negotiations on rules to begin, the United States made it clear in a working paper published in September – along with a handful of other countries including Russia and Israel – that it would block such a decision. Instead, it has proposed talks on guidelines to continue for another five years – a move NGOs have described as a further tactic to delay rules from ever being decided.
“Some states are weaponising consensus, on both procedural and substantive issues, to ensure that there will be no outcome this week,” Beatrice Fihn, founder and director of Lex International, and former executive director of the International Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons, said in a statement. “It’s really up to the rest of the world to decide how to get around these delay tactics,” she further told Geneva Solutions on the sidelines of the conference.

# Keeping the human in the loop

Autonomous weapons have long existed, for example, on warships as defence against incoming missiles. But new-generation AI-assisted weapons with increasing autonomy are emerging in conflicts, including in Sudan, Gaza and Ukraine, and experts are growing concerned at the prospect of handing over life-and-death decisions to machines as the technology behind them becomes ever more complex.
In a joint statement in August, UN secretary general António Guterres and International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) president Mirjana Spoljaric warned the weapons were “dangerously close to crossing a moral red line”, while at a recent meeting on AI at the Vatican, Pope Leo XIV also stressed that decisions on human life could never be given to machines.
Organisations like the ICRC stop short of calling for an outright ban on all lethal autonomous weapons but say those that target human beings, such as autonomous anti-personnel weapons, or that cannot guarantee predictability, should be outlawed in line with international humanitarian principles.
Read also: Killer robots close to breaching ‘moral red line’, warn UN and ICRC amid renewed push for treaty

# Campaigners weigh options

With the outcome of talks this week uncertain, countries and NGOs have been weighing up taking decisions outside of Geneva, where a consensus is needed – for example to the General Assembly – or even invoking an article of the CCW where a state or group of states can submit a proposal to the UN secretary general to negotiate a new protocol – although with Guterres’ term running out and no successor in sight – this could prove an unlikely option.
