**Title:** Auditing Learned Dynamics in Weather Models
**arXiv ID:** 2611.25119 (cs.LG)
**Authors:** Skylar Gu and Christina Last
**Submitted:** 18 November 2026

**GraphCast:** The paper describes GraphCast as "GraphCast, DeepMind's autoregressive weather forecasting model," and uses sparse autoencoder features from it.

**Mesh-feature ablation:** The authors report that "ablating a feature locked to GraphCast's computational mesh increases global geopotential height error." They note this holds even though the feature lacks conventional physical semantics.

**Convection and low-level-vorticity features:** Suppressing these features "weakens predicted tropical-cyclone deepening." Amplifying them reduces intensity error.

**Median error reduction:** Amplifying convection features through feature scaling achieves "a median of 51% error reduction over seven storms."

input.prompt: Give exact title, arXiv ID, authors, submission date. Quote exactly: the number of RL runs and model sizes, the "capitals of former states" finding including the 98% figure and the eleven-of-twelve detail, the hand-changed-verdicts figure (5% to 90%), the matched-leniency figure (two of four judges, 38-42%), and the "I don't know" blocked figure (94%).

response.result:
**Title:** Blind Spots Travel, Knowledge Stays Home: What RL Inherits from an LLM Judge
**arXiv ID:** 2611.25191 (cs.CL)
**Authors:** Liang Yue, Eric A. Vance
**Submitted:** 18 November 2026

**Key findings:**

- **Scale:** The authors ran 814 RL runs training 7-8B models. The paper describes them as teaching the models to "answer closed-book questions or abstain."
- **Capitals of former states:** A judge "rejects eleven of the twelve correct training answers about capitals of former states." This teaches the model to refuse 98% of such capitals on new questions, a loss that accuracy and abstention rates do not reveal.
- **Hand-changed verdicts:** Changing only those twelve verdicts by hand moves refusal "from 5% to 90%," even for a grader that accepts as many answers as the answer key.
- **Matched leniency:** At that leniency, two of four judges already cost 38-42% of these capitals.
- **"I don't know" blocked:** With that option blocked, the model answers 94% of the capitals correctly, so the knowledge is retained rather than forgotten.

The authors conclude that a grader doesn't need its own knowledge. Rewarding the model for the answer most of its untrained samples agree on, with no labels and no judge, matches the answer key's reward and preserves the category.

**Title:** Why Do LLMs Help with Scientific Misconduct Requests and What to Do About It?: Increasing the Trustworthiness of AI for Science

**arXiv ID:** 2611.25492 (cs.AI)

**Authors:** Almene De Meran Meguimtsop, Daniel E. Acuna

**Submitted:** 19 November 2026 (v1)

**Key findings:**

- **Models:** 8 LLMs were tested on SciIntBench, a benchmark of 1,350 prompts about scientific research integrity.

**Paper details**
- **Title:** "Pandora's Toolbox Or Why Agent Safety Cannot Be Verified"
- **arXiv ID:** 2611.25325 (cs.AI)
- **Authors:** Mario Franco and Carlos Gershenson
- **Submitted:** 19 Nov 2026 (v1)

**Key claims**

- **Undecidability:** The authors "show that this coupling makes safety undecidable." They state that "no algorithm can predict whether an agent will run such a program" that is semantically equivalent to a dangerous one.

- **PSPACE-completeness and finite constraints:** Under finite limits, "safety is decidable but still intractable." Specifically, "the problem is PSPACE-complete even when the description of the agent is known." The finite constraints are bounded context, values, and running time.

- **Non-compositionality:** The paper says "safety is not a compositional property." It notes that "agents that can be proven safe on their own can still produce unsafe behavior when grouped together."

- **Guardrails, blacklists, whitelists, and certifications:** The abstract states that "guardrails, blacklists, whitelists and certifications can only lead to imperfect safety solutions."

response.result:
**Title:** AI Deactivation Reduces Loneliness and Increases Social Interaction

**arXiv ID:** 2611.25263 (cs.HC; cross-listed cs.CY)

**Authors:** Dora Zhao, Grace Wang, Yutong Zhang, Lujain Ibrahim, Robert E. Kraut, Diyi Yang

**Submission date:** 18 November 2026 (v1)

**Sample size:** N = 625 active ChatGPT users.

**Treatment and control:** Participants were randomly assigned to abstain from AI assistants for fourteen days (treatment) or one day (control).

**Loneliness:** Two weeks of deactivation "significantly reduced loneliness relative to the control group" (β = -0.10, p = 0.03). The page reports only this regression coefficient, not a standardized effect size.

**Persistence:** The reduction persisted two weeks after participants resumed AI use (β = -0.16, p = 0.02).

**Productivity use case:** 84.7% of participants reported productivity as their most frequent use of AI.

**Social interaction:**
- Deactivation significantly increased the number of people participants interacted with in person.
- It significantly increased the time participants spent socializing over the intervention period.
- In open-ended responses, participants said they asked other people for help with tasks they would otherwise have delegated to AI, and they redirected their attention toward social interaction.

PHP on Thursday rolled out a fresh set of security patches as part of its four-week update schedule, including fixes for seven critical-severity remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities.

First in line is CVE-2026-115560 , which was publicly disclosed last month, two days after PHP2Shell patches landed. Residing in the session upload progress feature, it could be triggered to write attacker data using one session serialization format and then read it using another.

“A mismatched decoder can interpret part of a session key as serialized object data. An application with a suitable object gadget chain can then execute code with the privileges of the PHP worker,” PHP’s advisory reads.

Next in line is CVE-2026-129481 , described as a use-after-free that occurs after a session shutdown has been interrupted, and which PHP describes as an incomplete fix for CVE-2026-109619, one of the two PHP2Shell flaws fixed in October and now widely exploited.

“An attacker who can cause an application’s session cleanup to fail in this way may corrupt memory or crash a reused PHP worker. The use-after-free could potentially lead to remote code execution, but code execution through this specific field has not been demonstrated,” PHP notes, adding that PHP 8.2 is not affected.

Another use-after-free, CVE-2026-129182 , covers additional exploitation scenarios for CVE-2026-109619, an RCE via stale global state. According to PHP, however, RCE via these scenarios has not been demonstrated. Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Impacting PHP 8.5 and later, CVE-2026-129474 is a use-after-free weakness that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to cause a fatal error and achieve RCE. “Exploitation depends on the application and requires control over enough request data to influence memory allocation, a reachable magic method call, and a fatal error at the relevant point,” PHP says.

Attackers able to influence session contents and interrupt the write of serialized data to a session file may trigger the deserialization of attacker-controlled content when the session is next opened. Tracked as CVE-2026-126714 , the flaw could lead to RCE via a suitable object gadget chain in the application.

PHP also patched CVE-2026-129289 , a PHP-FPM request smuggling issue caused by PHP reading a request-body stream lazily, treating a request body as handled during request shutdown and skipping the normal cleanup that discards unread input.

“PHP can fail to discard unread bytes from an HTTP request body before reusing a persistent PHP-FPM or LSAPI connection. In PHP-FPM, an unauthenticated attacker can make those bytes form a separate FastCGI request, bypass front-end routing and execute attacker-controlled PHP code with the privileges of the worker,” PHP explains.

The seventh critical-severity vulnerability patched today, CVE-2026-129496 , resides in the timezone cache. PHP can retain a reference to it when writing a diagnostic to a PHP error log file during process startup, and a later diagnostic can access the freed cache before it is reset.

“On affected configurations, a remote attacker can trigger memory corruption, cause a worker to crash, and potentially execute arbitrary code with the privileges of the PHP worker,” PHP explains.

PHP 8.6.0 and PHP 8.5.13 were rolled out with fixes for all critical bugs and for 10 high and medium-severity flaws. Patches for most issues were also included in PHP 8.4.28, PHP 8.3.37, and PHP 8.2.36. More information is available on PHP’s news archive page.

The PHP Foundation has released security patches for a new set of 18 vulnerabilities , seven of which are marked critical.

These vulnerabilities affect all supported PHP versions but require either non-default configuration or uncommon setups to be exploited.

This set of newly disclosed PHP vulnerabilities come a month after the disclosure of two critical flaws in PHP, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and collectively known as ‘PHP2Shell.’

This was not merely a theoretical risk. In the weeks following the disclosure, security researchers began documenting real-world exploitation attempts and compromises involving internet-facing systems, demonstrating the potential consequences of leaving vulnerable PHP installations unpatched.

For example, Check Point reported campaigns exploiting PHP2Shell against its own security gateways , dating back to 30 October. The attacks involved the deployment of backdoors and even destructive tools targeting VMware ESXi virtualisation servers.

The exploitation activity also extended to Palo Alto Networks firewalls , with attackers targeting devices whose administrative interfaces were exposed to the internet.

Of the flaws published in the November update one is a remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in session upload progress, tracked as CVE-2026-115560. It was disclosed by PHP on October 23 , two days after PHP released emergency fixes for the critical PHP2Shell vulnerabilities. It has been noted that exploitation of this vulnerability requires a highly specific and unlikely combination of conditions.

#
PHP Session Handling Flaws Enable Remote Code Execution

One of the new critical flaws, dubbed ‘PHPAfterShell ’ and tracked as CVE-2026-126714, was discovered by security firm Depthfirst using AI frontier models tuned for cybersecurity tasks.

The vulnerability lives in PHP’s session handling with file-based storage, the default (session.save_handler = files).

By exploiting a flaw in this process, an attacker can manipulate a session while a file is being uploaded, potentially tricking the server into executing arbitrary code.

Successful exploitation could allow a remote attacker access to sensitive information, including login credentials and customer records, modify session data, spy on visitors or disrupt the affected service.

It affects the following versions:

-
PHP 8.5 < 8.5.13

-
PHP 8.4 < 8.4.28

-
PHP 8.3 < 8.3.37

-
PHP 8.2 < 8.2.36

-
PHP 8.1 and earlier are end-of-life

#
PHP Security Patches Address 16 Additional Vulnerabilities

The other vulnerabilities addressed in PHP’s 19 November 2026 security release include the following:

-

-
CVE-2026-129474 (CVSS 9.2): a use-after-free flaw in magic method backtraces that could allow attackers to execute arbitrary code

-
CVE-2026-129182 (CVSS 9.2): a use-after-free vulnerability involving the repopulation of the last fatal error backtrace after shutdown, potentially leading to remote code execution

-
CVE-2026-129496 (CVSS 9.2): a use-after-free vulnerability in the time zone cache that could potentially lead to remote code execution

-
CVE-2026-129501 (CVSS 6.3): a double-free vulnerability during DOM XML serialization that can cause memory corruption and denial of service

-
CVE-2026-129538 (CVSS 6.9): an out-of-bounds read and write vulnerability in PHP-CGI when correcting the PATH_INFO environment variable, potentially resulting in memory corruption

-

-
CVE-2026-129289 (CVSS 9.2): a request-smuggling vulnerability caused by unread HTTP request bodies, potentially allowing attackers to manipulate how requests are processed

Fresh security updates for the Ruby programming language resolve seven vulnerabilities in its regular expression engine and in the case conversion of strings. Proof-of-concept (PoC) code demonstrating remote code execution (RCE) exists for five of them.

At the top of the list sits CVE-2026-132825 (CVSS score of 7.4), described as a heap-based buffer overflow in the case conversion of strings that could potentially lead to RCE in certain scenarios.

Dubbed Ruby2Shell , the flaw impacts character case-conversion operations. In some single-byte encodings, including ISO-8859-1 and Windows-1252, when changing the case of a string, Ruby may end up writing one byte past the output buffer.

“For example, converting the German character ß to uppercase produces SS. In affected code, Ruby checks that sufficient space exists for one byte but writes two, potentially corrupting adjacent heap memory,” Previdian explains.

Veria Labs reports that, in default Ruby configurations, unauthenticated attackers could trigger the security defect from Rails, classic-style Sinatra, and potentially other frameworks.

According to preemptive exposure management firm WatchTowr , “any Ruby application that changes the case of external text in a single-byte encoding” is affected by the vulnerability. Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

According to Veria Labs, which plans to release a PoC after major vendors have rolled out patches, GitHub Enterprise Server is affected. Chatwoot, GitLab, Mastodon, OpenProject, and the Discourse base image have patched the bug.

Successful exploitation of Ruby2Shell in production environments is likely to be challenging, WatchTowr principal threat intelligence specialist Yordan Ganchev told SecurityWeek .

According to him, correctly laying out memory is difficult, and “attackers would also need the right non-glibc memory allocator, runtime configuration, and application logic preconditions, making exploitation even more challenging.”

“And if that weren’t enough, they’d need to contend with anyone else hammering the system on the internet and, in the end, defeat Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), making the whole journey a complete odyssey,” Ganchev noted.

Most likely, malformed requests could lead to denial-of-service (DoS) and service disruption, he said.

The other four vulnerabilities with a PoC demonstrating RCE include a double free, two integer overflows, and a heap-based buffer overflow. CVE identifiers for these issues have been requested but not assigned yet. PoC code also exists for an out-of-bounds read, demonstrating memory corruption.

Ruby also resolved an out-of-bounds read in its regular expression engine that could lead to memory leaks and process crashes.

Patches for all seven vulnerabilities were included in Ruby versions 4.0.10, 3.4.13, or 3.3.14. Users are advised to apply the fixes as soon as possible.

- /home/user/ainews/data/2026-11-20.json  (the edition)
- /home/user/ainews/data/2026-11-20.script.json  (the podcast script, derived from the edition)

The script is only allowed to say what the edition says. Your job:

For every statement in the script, find the sentence in the edition that supports it. List every statement that is not supported, adds a detail, changes a number, softens or drops a caveat, or characterises something the edition does not — quote the script line and the closest edition text. If everything is supported, reply exactly: NO UNSUPPORTED STATEMENTS.

Notes on what is legitimately allowed, so you don't report false positives:
- The intro may use facts and numbers from the edition's `summary` array.
- The intro's fixed show furniture is allowed and needs no support: the spoken date, "this is The AI Edge, presented by Epilogue", the two sentences about Epilogue and "epiloguelabs.com", the hosts' names ("I'm Maya", "And I'm Alex"), and one or two lines of generic framing about what happened at the frontier of AI since yesterday morning.
- The outro's furniture is allowed and needs no support: wrapping up, saying the full edition and its source links are on the site, "Our voices are AI-generated", and inviting listeners back tomorrow.
- Short conversational connective lines and questions that carry no facts ("And the finding?", "What was actually hit?", "To what end?") need no support.
- Transition lines that carry no facts are allowed.
- Rewording for speech is allowed as long as the fact and the caveat are unchanged — e.g. "3 to 6%" for "3-6%", "seven of them critical" for "seven of them marked critical", "a severity score of 9.2" for "CVSS 9.2".

Be strict about: numbers that differ from the edition, named entities the edition does not name, attributions to a publisher the edition does not credit for that fact, causal or evaluative claims the edition does not make, and caveats present in the edition's bullets but weakened or missing in the script.

Report findings as a numbered list, each with: the script line quoted, the closest edition text quoted, and one sentence saying what is wrong. Do not fix anything. Do not write any files.

input.message:
Checked every script line against the edition (`/home/user/ainews/data/2026-11-20.json` vs `/home/user/ainews/data/2026-11-20.script.json`).

Good news first, so the caller knows what I cleared: every number in the script matches the edition exactly (111.50 / 97.17 / 17% / $83 / 879,000 / 3.4m / 7,400 / 26-59% / 3-6% / 68-97% / 59-87% / 13% / 94.1% / 25.9% / 68.0% / 125 / 18 flaws / seven critical / CVSS 9.2 / 11 models / 93% F1 / one in four / 51% / seven storms / 63% / 1.5h→30min / 4h→1.5h / 1,200 / 15min / 26 members / 7 Republicans / 45% / 11.9m / 21.7m / 35% / 24.8TWh / 18-16-25% / 114.99 / 34% / 550 / 1,100 / 2% / $1.76tn / 14.48% / 30% / 31% / $64.6bn / 7.06% / 9.21% / 5.92% / 7.01% / 5.21% / 4.76% / 6.37% / 2.67% / 5.43% / 625 / 84.7%). Every named entity, outlet attribution and quote in the script appears in the edition's bullets or `summary`, attributed to the same source. No causal or evaluative claim is invented beyond the edition's own framing (e.g. "CNBC ties the sell-off to…" and "the listing steadied nothing" both track edition text).

Findings, most serious first:

1. **PHP item — exploitability caveat dropped, and the script's framing points the other way.**
   Script: `"How exposed does that leave people?"` → `"It sits in PHP's session handling with file-based storage, which is the default."`
   Edition: "The PHP Foundation released patches for 18 vulnerabilities, seven of them marked critical, affecting all supported PHP versions but requiring \"either non-default configuration or uncommon setups to be exploited,\" Infosecurity Magazine reports."
   The script asks the exposure question and answers only with the "which is the default" detail, dropping the edition's explicit caveat that exploitation requires non-default configuration or uncommon setups — the one caveat that actually answers the question, and its omission makes the batch sound more exposed than the edition says.

2. **Oxford mental-health item — the edition's second caveat is replaced by a generic one.**
   Script: `"It's a preprint, so it hasn't been peer reviewed, and it rests on a single source."`
   Edition: "The paper is a preprint and has not been peer reviewed; the authors do not report testing the five developers' own crisis-routing features separately from the model responses."
   The script keeps the preprint caveat but drops the substantive limitation that the study did not test the developers' own crisis-routing features separately, so the low percentages are presented as a cleaner measure of real-world safeguarding than the edition allows.

3. **Loneliness trial — the caveat attached to the 84.7% figure is dropped.**
   Script: `"84.7% of participants named productivity as their most frequent use case, so this isn't a study of companion chatbots. It's a preprint resting on a single source, and the effects are small regression coefficients."`
   Edition: "84.7% of participants named productivity as their most frequent use case… The paper is a preprint; the effect sizes are small regression coefficients, and the abstract page and v1 HTML differ slightly on that participation figure."
   The script states 84.7% flatly and carries the other two caveats, but drops the edition's note that the abstract page and v1 HTML disagree on that very figure.

4. **GraphCast item — the 51% figure is attached to a broader intervention than the edition reports.**
   Script: `"Suppressing features associated with convection and low-level vorticity weakened the predicted deepening of tropical cyclones. Amplifying them reduced intensity error, with a median of 51% error reduction over seven storms."`
   Edition: "while amplifying them reduces intensity error, with amplification of convection features through feature scaling achieving \"a median of 51% error reduction over seven storms.\""
   The edition ties the 51% specifically to amplification of convection features through feature scaling; the script's "Amplifying them" refers back to both convection and low-level-vorticity features and omits the feature-scaling method, broadening what produced the result.

5. **UK social care item — the guidance's legal status and territorial scope are dropped.**
   Script: `"The UK published what it calls the first ever cross-sector guidance on the use of AI in children's and adult social care, issued on GOV.UK by the Department of Health and Social Care and the Department for Education."`
   Edition: "…published what they call the \"First ever cross-sector guidance on the use of artificial intelligence in children's and adult social care\" — non-statutory guidance for England setting out principles on governance, accountability, data protection and professional oversight."
   "Non-statutory" and "for England" are both dropped, so the script presents a UK-wide, unqualified publication where the edition specifies non-binding guidance covering England only.

6. **PHP item — exploitation campaigns broadened beyond Check Point's own gateways.**
   Script: `"Infosecurity does note that campaigns against the October PHP flaws have been hitting security gateways since October 30th, including destructive tools aimed at VMware ESXi servers."`
   Edition: "Infosecurity says Check Point reported campaigns exploiting PHP2Shell against its own security gateways dating back to 30 October, involving backdoors and destructive tools targeting VMware ESXi servers…"
   The edition's scope is Check Point reporting attacks against its own security gateways; the script's unattributed "hitting security gateways" generalises this to security gateways at large.

7. **Cache side-channel item — a hedge is removed.**
   Script: `"an agent's tools run on your own machine and share system libraries"`
   Edition: "tools \"are executed on the user's machine and commonly rely on shared system libraries\""
   "Commonly rely on" becomes an unqualified "share", stating the precondition for the attack as universal rather than common.

8. **Loneliness trial — the measurement window for the social effects is dropped.** (minor)
   Script: `"It also increased the number of people they interacted with in person and the time they spent socialising."`
   Edition: "Deactivation \"also significantly increased the number of people participants interacted with in person and the time they spent socializing over the intervention period.\""
   "Over the intervention period" is omitted, and because the preceding script sentence describes loneliness effects persisting two weeks after resumption, the social effects can be read as persisting too.

Everything else — the intro's three headline facts (all drawn from `summary`), the show furniture, all transitions, and the Amodei, CAPTCHA, European Commission, ToolPulse, House committee, caucus, Meta, Anthropic IPO and SoftBank items — is supported by edition text, with the caveat lines in those items matching the edition's own.

What happened in frontier AI — Friday, 20 November 2026

Anthropic began trading on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, opening at $111.50 — about 34% above its $83 IPO price — reaching as high as $114.99 and closing at $97.17, up 17%.

• Amodei tells Nasdaq opening bell Anthropic will pace training and deployment and stay under human control
• Oxford study: models met mental-health safeguarding standards in 3-6% of conversations when distress cues were dispersed
• European Commission confirms October attack on its personnel systems was an "AI-generated cyber campaign"
• House committee publishes licence records showing BIS approved more than 879,000 AI chips for Chinese buyers
• Merck and Isomorphic Labs sign small-molecule oncology discovery deal with no disclosed financial terms
• US Senate passes energy permitting and transmission bill 62-33, with warnings about data centre power
• Meta reevaluates its 2030 net-zero timeline after net carbon footprint rose 45% to 11.9 million tonnes

One thing worth fixing: today's publish was delayed ~25 minutes because my own trace commits kept cancelling the deploy workflow. deploy.yml's concurrency group cancels in-progress runs, so each "git add trace/ && push" after the edition commit killed the run that was building the site. A stop hook in this environment nags for uncommitted changes on every turn, which made me push repeatedly. Worth either excluding trace-only pushes from deploy.yml's trigger (paths-ignore: trace/**) or setting cancel-in-progress: false.

Also: Reuters, The Guardian, Channel NewsAsia, The Verge, Politico and Infosecurity Magazine were all blocked by the egress policy or 403 on WebFetch today — I worked around each with sources I could actually open, but that list is growing.

last_message:
Today's edition is published and the email is sent.

## Report — AI Edge Briefing, Friday 20 November 2026

**Window:** 19 Nov 12:40 → 20 Nov 11:05 UTC

**Items:** 29, across all eight sections — Frontier models & labs (2), Research & papers (6), Security misuse & threat intelligence (5), Military defense & geopolitics (2), Health science & medicine (2), Policy regulation & law (4), Compute chips & infrastructure (4), Deployment & impact (4).

**Storylines filed under:** `ai-enabled-hacking` (3), `compute-money` (3), `china-distillation-export-controls` (2), `pacing-frontier-ai` (1), `regulating-frontier-ai-us` (1). No new ids coined.

**Validation:** `validate.js --check-links` → 29 items, 39 links, 0 errors, 0 warnings. Script → 23 blocks, 14 items voiced, 2,296 words, 0 errors, 0 warnings. The adversarial fact-check found 8 real problems on round 1 (dropped caveats and broadened scope — the PHP exploitability caveat, the Oxford crisis-routing limitation, the loneliness figure discrepancy, the GraphCast 51% attribution, "non-statutory"/"England" on the UK guidance, Check Point's own gateways, "commonly rely on", and the intervention-period window). All fixed; round 2 returned **NO UNSUPPORTED STATEMENTS**. Script committed.

**Commit:** `bad499f` (edition), trace through `658bebc`. Pushed to `main`. Email sent to the reader with the built subject/html/text verbatim; edition, script and trace pages all return 200.

**Sources I could not reach:** Reuters, The Guardian, Channel NewsAsia, Morningstar/Dow Jones and The Verge (egress policy), Politico (egress policy, both WebFetch and fetch.js), Infosecurity Magazine and the Federal Register (403/redirect on WebFetch — Infosecurity opened via `fetch.js`, the Federal Register did not).

**Dropped for lack of verification or being outside the window:** the Frostbite AI-designed CPU and Anthropic's black-hole physics post (published 17–18 Nov; the latter already covered 10 Nov); Newsom's California AI framework, Genie 4's Ultra rollout and Microsoft's MAI Code 2 (all 17–18 Nov); OpenAI's Performance Factory post (19 Nov 08:00 GMT, before the window); the BIS Federal Register remote-access rule (could not open the document, and yesterday already carried the rule taking effect); Boltz's $110M Series A (sources disagreed on 18 vs 19 Nov); Byline Times' Palantir £240.6m figure (opinion column, time unverifiable); and a Reuters-sourced Meeks quote a beat returned that **did not match** the article when I checked it — I used only the verified wording.

**One thing to fix in the repo:** today's publish was delayed about 25 minutes by my own doing. `deploy.yml` uses a concurrency group that cancels in-progress runs, so each trace commit I pushed after the edition cancelled the run that was building the site — three times. A stop hook here nags about uncommitted changes every turn, which drove the repeated pushes. Adding `paths-ignore: trace/**` to deploy.yml's push trigger, or `cancel-in-progress: false`, would prevent it; I held the last trace commit back locally until the deploy finished rather than cancel it again.
